title: Twenty minutes' notice of Tasmanian job cuts, union says
text:
Tell us about your experience.

The state's public sector union has accused the Tasmanian government of "mishandling" the process to cut about 250 jobs, saying it's "without empathy" and leaving staff in tears.

"People are talking about this feeling like a massacre," Community and Public Sector Union (CPSU) state secretary Thirza White said, calling Tuesday a "brutal day".

Ms White said staff in Building Tasmania and the Department of Premier and Cabinet had been called into meetings with as little as 20 minutes' notice, and informed about job cuts in their teams.

"Some people walked in and were shown an organisational chart where their role wasn't on that … what we hear from others is that they're walking in and the team is six, and now the team is three," she said.

"What we have is a government and agencies that are drip-feeding information and what workers deserve and need is clarity around what the new structure is."

Thirza White says some staff received "as little as 20 minutes' notice" for meetings, before being informed about job cuts. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Forced job cuts loom as Tasmanian government prepares to swing axe About 150 Tasmanian public service jobs have been identified to be abolished as part of ongoing government efforts to shrink the state service.

The government is expected to release, on Wednesday afternoon, more detailed plans for the restructure, which has seen State Growth renamed Building Tasmania and slimmed its focus to infrastructure.

As pat of the process, many of its former functions have been transferred to the Department of Premier and Cabinet.

One hundred and eleven workers had already accepted voluntary redundancies, but staff were informed on Monday that another 150 jobs would be axed.

The workers will be offered voluntary redundancies or placed on the redeployment list, which could see them take another job or be let go after six months.

Ms White said the CPSU was expecting to receive organisational charts, and a list of required roles on Wednesday afternoon.

Kerry Vincent says "change is always difficult for some to adjust to". (ABC News: Jake Grant)

Minister yet to sight restructure plans

Asked what details would be made public on Wednesday morning, the minister responsible for Building Tasmania Kerry Vincent said he had not yet seen the documents.

He said it would include "some of the finer details".

"We, as always, are keen to work through with everybody involved to make sure that we are driving efficiencies through the public service."

Pressed on what exactly the finer details were, he said "the finer details are always on how things can operate efficiently for the benefit of Tasmanian taxpayers and that's what we're trying to do".

Mr Vincent pushed back on the suggestion the government had mishandled the process.

"I feel for everybody in the system because change is always difficult for some to adjust to," he said.

" But I ask everybody to keep an open mind to what we are trying to achieve here and work through it with us. "

Greens call for other measures, including axing stadium

The state budget outlines job cuts across the public service to help balance spending and revenue, targeting 1,700 by 2030, and another 100 by 2032.

Where are the cuts coming from in Tasmania's state budget? Treasurer Eric Abetz wants to find $1.47 billion in "efficiencies" in Tasmania's state budget. This is what's on the chopping block.

Treasurer Eric Abetz has repeatedly said that cutting expenditure is his preferred method for budget repair.

His May state budget included $1.5 billion in "operational efficiencies" over the next four years, with departments required to find the savings through slashing jobs or services.

Acting Greens Leader Vica Bayley called on the government to look at other measures, including raising new revenue and abandoning the Hobart stadium project at Macquarie Point.

"Salmon farming corporations, mining companies, property developers and the gambling industry are all getting an easy ride while public services and the Tasmanians who rely on them are paying the price," he said.

title: Umpire felt 'threatened' by player, fan abuse after unruly AFL finale
text:
A 34-year-old Seaford man is expected to be charged for allegedly throwing a plate of food at a woman and child during last week's AFL preliminary final between Hawthorn and Brisbane.

He is expected to be charged on summons with aggravated unlawful assault and discharge a missile.

AFL bans loom for bottle-throwing Hawks fans Hawthorn supporters who threw bottles at umpires after a controversial finals exit face lengthy bans if identified by the AFL and Victoria Police.

Police have interviewed the man and another 56-year-old Tullamarine man, who was identified after allegedly throwing a bottle onto the MCG's field of play at the conclusion of the match.

The Tullamarine man has been fined $418 under the Major Events Act.

He is the second man to be fined after security detained a 40-year-old Croydon man for throwing a bottle onto the field of play, before he was spoken to by police.

Bottles and cans were thrown onto the field after the game, including some aimed at the umpires as they walked off the MCG after a holding-the-ball decision by field umpire Hayden Meyer against Jarman Impey that gave Brisbane a go-ahead goal with 18 seconds remaining.

Umpire says he felt 'threatened' by Hawks duo

Sicily and Barrass (number 37) were seen having words with Meyer (left) immediately following the final siren. (AFL)

Meyer, who will officiate in this weekend's AFL grand final, was confronted by Hawthorn captain James Sicily and defender Tom Barrass in the aftermath of his decision.

He said he had received an apology from Barrass but was still waiting to hear from Sicily.

"The abuse that came my way, I felt threatened," Meyer told reporters on Wednesday.

"I expressed exactly that [to the AFL] — the language, and the way that those two players, James [Sicily] and Tom [Barrass], came at me, I felt threatened and intimidated in that situation.

"So I spoke to [umpires boss] Steve McBurney the day after and gave my view of the situation, and how I felt and what occurred, and he then transferred that to Swanny [AFL football boss Greg Swann] and the MRO to eventually come up with a decision around the fines.

"[Barrass] was very apologetic and very sincere in his apology. I accepted his apology and thanked him for taking the time out of his day to give me a call."

Meyer says Sicily (pictured) is yet to apologise for abusing him on the final siren. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Meyer refused to make a call on whether the Hawks pair, who were fined over their actions, should be suspended instead.

"That's out of my control, that's not my decision … I suppose what I take from it is that it's not a great look for junior umpires and kids that are sitting on the couch that we want to recruit into umpiring," he said.

"They see that after the game on the weekend and, if I'm sitting on the couch, I'd be like, 'Do I really want to go to my local umpiring community group and sign up to be an umpire?'

" That was the big disappointing thing for me, that we struggle with umpiring recruitment in local communities, and that doesn't help. "

Despite the protestations from Hawthorn fans, Impey admitted the umpires made the right call.

"It was the right decision," he told the Kick It Forward podcast at the Brownlow Medal on Monday night.

"Naturally, when you think there are 30-40 seconds to go, you try and hold it in go from there, but credit to Hayden.

"I hope there was no hate message towards him, so sending love to him."

Jarman Impey (left) admitted the umpires had made the right call in penalising him for holding the ball in the final seconds. (Getty Images: Josh Chadwick)

Ahead of this weekend's grand final, Meyer pleaded for fans to not "cross the line" again.

"I've never experienced bottles being thrown at me post-game. It was pretty scary, to be honest, and I hope it never happens again in any game, any sport," he said.

"[To fans attending the grand final], I would say be passionate, cheer for your team, but respect others, respect the people you're sitting next to, respect the umpires — have fun, but don't cross the line."

Police are continuing to make enquiries regarding the fan behaviour during and after the match.

title: Coalition vows to 'take a chainsaw' to climate laws, offshore wind
text:
Tell us about your experience.

The Coalition has vowed to abolish most of Australia's "offshore wind zones" if it wins government, massively limiting where wind farms can be built, as part of a commitment for a major slowdown of the nation's energy transition.

Shadow Energy Minister Dan Tehan said revoking the offshore wind zones along the Hunter, Illawarra, Southern Ocean and Bunbury coasts would be part of an eight-point plan to unpick Australia's key climate policies.

"We will take a chainsaw to Labor's ideologically driven, energy-restrictive approach to energy," Mr Tehan will say in an address to The Australian's energy summit.

As well as winding back the offshore wind rollout, the Coalition would also repeal laws committing Australia to reach net zero emissions by 2050, remove laws requiring the nation's biggest polluters to cut their emissions or face penalties and remove laws requiring car makers to provide more efficient vehicles to Australia, including electric vehicles.

The Coalition would also attempt to lift the prohibition on nuclear power — though that would require laws to be passed by the Senate, where there is no chance for the Coalition to win support without either Labor or the Greens changing positions on nuclear energy.

Dan Tehan says he wants to take a chainsaw to Labor's climate policies. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The power plan formalises the Coalition's abandonment of most of the major policies attempting to drive down carbon emissions and speed up the transition of Australia's electricity networks from coal towards renewable power.

"Within 30 days of getting into government we will introduce the scrap net zero bill … which will get rid of Labor's egregious taxes across energy in our country, taxes on vehicles, it will get rid of the vehicle emissions standards … it will get rid of the safeguard mechanism, which is sending industry offshore," Mr Taylor said.

While the Coalition is vowing to unpick most of the measures being used to cut emissions, the party says it remains committed to addressing climate change, but says the cost of energy to home owners and industry should be put first.

The CSIRO says solar and wind power remain cheaper power sources than coal, even after accounting for transmission costs.

However, the pace of transition has been slower than intended, and has required major investment support through the government's Capacity Investment Scheme.

The Coalition says that scheme should not be picking winners, and should also be allowed to underwrite coal, gas and nuclear power.

Energy Minister Chris Bowen said the Coalition's plan would "take a chainsaw" to the economy and household budgets.

"It will make Australia poorer, weaker and less secure from global shocks," Mr Bowen said.

"Their plan to stop renewables and household batteries, and sweat coal, would mean Aussie households are left to pick up the bill of global shocks."

Coalition would unpick nascent offshore wind industry

While the Coalition says Australia should have "energy abundance", it has vowed to cancel most of the declared offshore wind zones which have been opened for potential investment.

Repealing four of Australia's six offshore wind zones would leave Gippsland in Victoria and the Bass Strait in Tasmania as the only approved coasts for wind farms.

Mr Tehan was supportive of offshore wind when he joined Energy Minister Chris Bowen at the announcement of the Southern Ocean offshore wind zone in 2023, which is within his federal electorate of Wannon.

"The scale of these offshore wind farms is something to behold, and it's going to need all the community coming together to make sure that we benefit from it … we want to make sure that it continues and continues to provide jobs, and offshore wind can provide that," Mr Tehan said at the time.

Wannon MP Dan Tehan joined Energy Minister Chris Bowen to offer support for the Southern Ocean offshore renewable energy zone when it was first being consulted on. (Supplied)

Since then, the party has abandoned many of the climate commitments it signed up to under former prime minister Scott Morrison, as high industrial gas costs put pressure on Australian industry, and high power bills stress households — both of which the Coalition blames on limits put on coal and gas.

While offshore wind is an established industry overseas, particularly in Europe and China, the industry is still developing in Australia.

The Albanese government identified six regions as priority areas for offshore wind to help kick-start the industry, opening space for developers to conduct feasibility and environmental studies and begin community consultation.

There are no active wind farms or projects under construction, though about a dozen projects have been granted licences to begin planning.

Offshore wind can harness stronger and more consistent winds than onshore farms, while avoiding taking up valuable agricultural land.

But they are also much more expensive than onshore wind, disrupt marine life during construction as well as fishing activities, and have faced resistance in some communities neighbouring the offshore zones.

The Coalition's eight energy priorities Read more Read more Repeal the Climate Change Act 2022, which commits Australia to net zero emissions by 2050. Remove the safeguard mechanism, which requires heavy industry to cut emissions or face penalties. Repeal the New Vehicle Efficiency Standard, which requires car makers to import more fuel-efficient and electric vehicles or face penalties. Revoke four offshore wind energy zones across the Hunter, Illawarra, Southern Ocean and Bunbury regions. Repeal all legislative prohibitions on nuclear energy. Introduce a renewable energy code of conduct "to ensure developers earn their social licence from the community that they operate in". Require that any energy funding provided to the states and territories is conditional on prioritising energy affordability and reliability. Redirect the Australian Energy Regulator to have primary regard to affordability and reliability, which will put households and businesses at the centre of regulatory decision-making.

The Coalition argues the offshore wind push has failed, with no projects under construction four years after the first wind zone was declared, adding that the government was forced to commit about $50 million last year in financial relief for stalled proposals.

United States President Donald Trump's moves to cancel funding and permits for offshore wind projects also cooled global investment.

The energy minister conceded in his National Press Club address in August that offshore wind was reducing in cost more slowly than previously predicted.

"Offshore wind has faced structural constraints around the world which make starting the industry from scratch harder than it would otherwise be," Mr Bowen said.

The minister noted that offshore wind was never expected to contribute to the government's 2030 goal of 82 per cent of power coming from renewables, and the government remained focused on delivering that renewables power, "while keeping our eye over the horizon".

Chris Bowen has acknowledged that offshore wind is progressing more slowly than hoped for. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The only measure in the Coalition's priority list that would encourage renewable power is a renewed pitch to lift the ban on nuclear power, which is prohibited under state and federal laws.

The Coalition argues states may want to reconsider those bans as energy-hungry AI data centres roll out across the country, saying the stable renewables source would become a much more realistic option.

However it will not re-adopt the proposal by former opposition leader Peter Dutton for the federal government to fund and part-own those nuclear plants — instead suggesting the only taxpayer support they would receive would be the same that is made available to any other energy source, such as through a reworked Capacity Investment Scheme.

Independent MP Monique Ryan said the Coalition's proposal was "dumb, dangerous and desperate" and would make energy more expensive.

"Australians have embraced clean energy because it works. We've spent years investing in rooftop solar, electric vehicles, household batteries and home electrification because these technologies save money and reduce emissions," Ms Ryan said.

"The Liberals' retrograde attempt to appease the Nationals and woo One Nation voters would drag the country backwards."

title: McGowan set to get director spot on Stokes-backed media giant
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Former WA premier Mark McGowan is tipped to be appointed to the board of media behemoth Southern Cross Media Group, following a merger with Kerry Stokes' Seven West Media.

Mr McGowan stepped down from public office in 2023 citing exhaustion after steering the state through the COVID pandemic.

He was a sometime political ally of billionaire Kerry Stokes, who controls a 23 per cent stake in Southern Cross, which is chaired by his son Ryan.

If successful, Mr McGowan will join a handful of political leaders who have accepted board seats on listed media companies, including former Victorian premier Jeff Kennett, who was previously a director of Seven West Media, and former prime minister Tony Abbott, who joined the board of the Murdochs' Fox Corporation in the US.

The ABC understands former senior Google and Twitter executive Karen Stocks is also in line to be appointed, subject to background checks on both candidates, which are being conducted by board search firm Hattonneale.

If successful both would still face election at the upcoming annual general meeting of Southern Cross, likely to be held in November.

The base rate for non-executive directors was $135,000 per year in 2025-2026.

Kerry Stokes's son Ryan Stokes (left) has recently been appointed chair of Southern Cross Media. (AAP: Mick Tsikas)

Mr McGowan and Southern Cross did not respond to questions, but it is understood announcement of the board appointments was planned for later this week.

Southern Cross, which also owns The West Australian newspaper and the Triple M and Hit commercial radio networks, is expanding its board in line with a charter adopted after it acquired Seven West Media for $385 million in shares, effective from January this year.

Kerry Stokes conglomerate Seven Group Holdings emerged with a 20 per cent minority stake in Southern Cross, which it lifted to 23 per cent via another Stokes' affiliated entity after six months as is allowed under the so-called creep provisions in the corporate takeover laws.

"Kerry Stokes is a master of the creep provision," said one finance industry source, pointing to his previous takeovers of Seven and The West Australian.

Earlier this month, after non-executive chair Teresa Dyson stepped down, Ryan Stokes took over the chairmanship, cementing his family's control of the merged entity.

Ex-ministers exert level of influence above ordinary people

The Centre for Public Integrity chair Anthony Whealy KC said the appointment could raise integrity concerns, given Mr McGowan's strong former connection to the WA government.

"Clearly with Mr McGowan there's been a number of years since he was the premier, but nevertheless, there remains a concern because he was such an influential politician and so powerful and so important within the state of Western Australia that his position with the Stokes company [Southern Cross] gives him a particular connection to the Western Australian government and a particular way of influence that other people would not have," Mr Whealy said.

"Of course, we don't wish him any ill will, we don't wish him to have a life bereft of commercial enterprise, but nevertheless there is that impression created and that's where the danger to integrity lies."

Premier and media mogul's texts seen during trial

Mr McGowan's relationship with Kerry Stokes was examined during his 2022 defamation battle with coal billionaire Clive Palmer, which surfaced a series of text exchanges between the then-premier and the mining and media mogul.

The Federal Court heard Mr McGowan sent Mr Stokes a text message in August 2020 flagging the introduction of legislation that would prevent Mr Palmer pursuing commercial arbitration damages against the state for up to $30 billion over a historical mine tenement agreement, and promising to "call to discuss".

"Mark, well done. I think no-one else could have achieved the legislation in the speed you did," Mr Stokes wrote back after the bill had been pushed through.

The exchange followed a series of front-page articles in Mr Stokes's state daily metro masthead, The West Australian, which depicted Mr Palmer variously as a cockroach and a cane toad, which were not the subject of the defamation claim.

Clive Palmer was depicted as Dr Evil and a cockroach on The West Australian front pages. (Supplied: The West Australian)

Mr McGowan replied to Mr Stokes:

"Thanks Kerry I was asked about those marvellous front pages today, and I said, 'I think The West has gone a bit soft'. I appreciate the support enormously."

The court ultimately found Mr Palmer and Mr McGowan had defamed each other, with Mr Palmer awarded $5,000 and Mr McGowan $20,000 in damages.

After that decision was handed down, Mr McGowan was asked about his relationship with Mr Stokes and the text exchange.

Mr McGowan said he rarely contacted Mr Stokes and had contact with many businesspeople in his capacity as the minister for state development.

"I'm the treasurer, I was the minister for state development, and I'm the premier, so you could go through virtually every major company and every major investor in Western Australia, at some level, I've had contact with them," he told The Sydney Morning Herald in 2022.

"I find [Mr Stokes] to be an engaging and interesting person and a committed West Australian who has done a great many good things for the state."

McGowan granted Stokes-backed firm export deal

In 2020, shortly after exchanging the Palmer texts, Mr McGowan also announced a lucrative exemption for a gas development, backed by Mr Stokes, to rules banning onshore producers from exporting their product.

Under the change, the Waitsia project would be allowed to export up to 50 per cent of its gas production over a fixed period.

At the same time, the government tightened supply rules for other onshore producers, preventing them from selling their product to the east coast.

Waitsia, a joint venture with Stokes-linked Beach Energy and Japanese trading and infrastructure firm Mitsui, was touted by Mr MrGowan as a "shovel-ready" project that would create 200 jobs amid concerns about boosting economic activity in the state during the COVID-19 pandemic.

However, it has since faced delays, achieving its first gas production late last year.

The changes to the state's gas policy attracted criticism at the time from peak body Australian Energy Producers (formerly APPEA), which complained about a lack of consultation, while former Liberal premier Colin Barnett described the Waitsia deal as "unprecedented" special treatment.

The Waitsia second stage gas project was granted an exemption by the McGowan government. (Supplied)

Ryan Stokes is currently a director of Beach Energy, while Seven Group Holdings has been a substantial shareholder.

When the exemption was announced, Beach Energy's shares rose, prompting questions at the time about whether Mr McGowan met with Ryan or Kerry Stokes about the deal.

While initially declining to comment, in 2022 amid renewed scrutiny of the deal during a projected domestic gas shortfall, Mr McGowan said he did not recall any meeting in the lead-up to the announcement.

"No, to the best of my recollection, no," he told WA Today.

"You're talking about issues of a few years ago. We got a major project up that's giving us 50 per cent of the gas from it and hundreds of jobs and security in the gas supply."

He has also since defended the decision.

"It's all well and good now to … look back on it and say, 'You shouldn't have done this or that'. That's the situation that we were confronting as a state, and we saw was happening in Victoria and New York and Italy and Iran and Britain," he said.

"Millions of people dying, literally, in advanced Western countries, economies crashing, a world in chaos, and so we did what we had to do on the circumstances, and we got a major project that gives us 50 per cent gas, not 15 per cent gas [reservation policy that applies to offshore gas]."

Mr McGowan achieved wild popularity in Western Australia and oversaw a landslide win during his government's re-election in 2021, taking majority control of both houses and securing 53 of the Lower House's 59 seats.

Since leaving office he has also reportedly taken up a role with former federal treasurer Joe Hockey's consultancy firm, Bondi Partners, and consultancies with mining companies Mineral Resources and BHP.

He was reported to have parted ways with Mineral Resources earlier this year.

title: Watchdog again blocks sale of RAC WA insurance arm to east-coast giant
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Australia's competition watchdog has again blocked the sale of WA's largest insurer to an east-coast industry giant, reiterating the purchase would likely reduce competition in the state's insurance markets and drive up premiums.

The Royal Automobile Club of WA (RAC WA) announced in May 2025 it would enter into a 20-year "partnership" with Sydney-based Insurance Australia Group (IAG), in a deal worth $1.35 billion.

After the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) originally opposed the acquisition in December 2025, the two companies lodged applications for a reassessment.

The Automobile Club of Western Australia, which later became the RAC, began in 1905. (ABC News: West Matteeussen)

The ACCC conducted an "in-depth assessment" of the proposal, finding the deal would leave IAG in control of more than half of WA's motor vehicle and home and contents insurance markets and "would have the effect or likely effect of substantially lessening competition".

ACCC chair Gina Cass-Gottlieb said the acquisition would have seen premiums increase, though the ACCC had not calculated by how much.

Gina Cass-Gottlieb says the deal would lead to a significant increase in market concentration. (AAP: Lukas Coch)

"The potential for higher prices is significant," she told 102.5 ABC Perth.

"Competition is the key driver of keeping prices lower. We see that where there is less competition, there are higher prices, and also that there is the potential for … taking advantage of [market] position."

Public benefit vs detriment

IAG will now lodge a public benefit application with the ACCC, which will then decide whether any public benefit from the acquisition would outweigh the detriment.

It is the first time such an application has been made since the ACCC's new system for reviewing large mergers and acquisitions took effect on January 1, 2026.

IAG Managing Director and CEO Nick Hawkins said the sale would result in "long-term benefits for members, customers and communities across Western Australia".

The RAC said members would be better off under the acquisition. (Supplied: RAC)

"RAC will remain local and we'll invest in enhancements to benefit the member experience, and continue to deliver high-quality, competitive insurance products and services," he said.

RAC Group CEO Rob Slocombe agreed, saying RAC WA's current customers would fare better if they were underwritten by a national insurer.

"We continue to believe in the benefits of the proposed partnership with IAG, which would strengthen RAC's ability to respond to a changing insurance landscape and maintain a competitive offering for members," he said.

"By partnering with a national insurer, RAC can reduce the risk it carries alone, while continuing and expanding our focus on members, the WA community and RAC's broader services."

RACWA sells insurance operations to IAG RACWA has announced a 20-year deal with insurance company Insurance Australia Group, handing over its entire insurance underwriting business.

Ms Cass-Gottlieb said the ACCC did not agree with that view.

"We understand [RAC WA] is likely to face increased expenses in the future … which applies to all insurers, but our assessment is that would not impact [RAC WA's] financial and capital position to the extent that it would not continue to be an effective competitor," she told 102.5 ABC Perth.

Ms Cass-Gottlieb said if the public benefit application failed, the companies would still have recourse.

"IAG and [RAC WA] have the ability and right to seek a review in the Australian Competition Tribunal," she said.

"There is [a way to go yet]. We might be talking about this further, I think."

title: City of Perth plunged into more turmoil as CEO sacked
text:
Tell us about your experience.

The trouble-plagued City of Perth, which is under investigation by the local government watchdog amid ongoing governance concerns, has sacked its chief executive officer.

Mayor Bruce Reynolds read from a statement on Wednesday morning and said a special meeting of council last night had voted to "terminate Ms Reynolds' appointment, effective immediately", following an independent investigation.

He said it was a "confidential employment matter", the details of which would not be released, but the findings of the investigation were "sufficiently serious" to warrant her sacking.

Bruce Reynolds would not take questions from journalists when announcing the CEO's sacking. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

He refused to take questions from journalists.

The decision comes just a week after Local Government Inspector Tony Brown announced a three-month inquiry into the council, telling journalists there were "fractured working relationships and ongoing governance issues at the city".

'Toxic witch hunt'

Ms Reynolds said in a statement she was "shocked" to learn she had been sacked and would appeal the decision, which followed a four-month investigation she branded a "witch hunt".

"The allegations and investigation appear to me to be nothing more than a witch hunt designed to impinge my reputation and scapegoat me by an otherwise toxic council and likely cost the rate payers handsomely," she said.

The City of Perth has faced ongoing allegations of dysfunction and poor governance. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

She said the allegations against her were "individually trivial in nature" and hinted that she would have more to say about the council's dysfunction.

"The allegations and subsequent investigation process have exposed the factionalism between the views of elected members with personal agendas and the effective function of the administration of local government as a multimillion-dollar business," she said.

"The dysfunction and harmful behaviours at the City of Perth, in particular amongst the elected members, is no secret and having been bound by confidentiality throughout the investigation I am now able to speak freely about my experiences and challenging relationship with certain members of council and intend to do so."

Ms Reynolds was sacked at a special meeting of council last night. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Ms Reynolds, who is not related to the mayor, was suspended from her job in May when the investigation into her began.

Mr Reynolds said council would now put interim leadership arrangements in place while a recruitment process began for a new CEO.

"We remain focused on the City, its people and the community we serve," he said.

Local Government Minister Hannah Beazley said the local government inspector would review the process that led to Ms Reynolds being sacked as part of his probe into the council.

"I have made it very clear that I have zero tolerance for dysfunction, zero tolerance for poor governance and zero tolerance for unsustainable financial management," she said.

title: Lions confirm they will appeal Neale's grand final ban
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Lachie Neale has one last hope of playing in the grand final after the Brisbane Lions chose to appeal his one-match suspension.

An appeals board hearing is the final avenue available for Neale, who unsuccessfully challenged the ban at a tribunal hearing last night.

The Lions announced this afternoon they would appeal the tribunal's decision.

Neale has travelled to Melbourne with the Lions squad. The appeals board hearing will be held tomorrow, beginning at 4pm, AEST.

To succeed at the appeals board hearing, the Lions will have to prove the tribunal finding was either an error of law, an unreasonable decision, a manifestly excessive classification, or a manifestly excessive sanction.

They face Fremantle in Saturday's grand final at the MCG, chasing a third successive premiership.

Neale was suspended after the tribunal rejected his "inconsistent" evidence in a landmark case.

Why Neale's grand final ban was upheld The tribunal says it had reason not to overturn Lachie Neale's appeal. Now the AFL world waits to hear whether the Lions will launch an appeal.

He was found guilty of striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan in Saturday night's preliminary final.

The two-time premiership captain argued his action was not a strike, but a body-check.

After a dramatic four-and-a-half-hour hearing, the tribunal upheld the charge and dismissed pleas for a downgrade due to exceptional and compelling circumstances.

The off-the-ball blow on Ginnivan was graded as intentional conduct, medium impact and body contact by match review officer Michael Christian.

Neale argued contact was made with his shoulder and chest and was not a strike.

He said Ginnivan "might have taken a bit of a dive to get a free kick".

"My shoulder made contact with his body and shoulder first and my arm wrapped around Jack," he said.

"But I didn't feel like I was striking him at all. It was more a bump or body-check."

The Lions will roll the dice on Lachie Neale's ban at an appeals board hearing. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Robert Cianflone)

But tribunal chair Jeff Gleeson KC dismissed Neale's version of events.

"We find that this was a forceful blow delivered with a swinging arm and an open hand," Gleeson said.

"When played at normal speed, it appears clear to us that this was, to use the common vernacular, a strike to the guts.

"We are comfortably satisfied that this is what occurred. We find that this is what Neale intended.

"We have listened carefully to Mr Neale's evidence but we find it was inconsistent in key respects with what we saw on the video and, to that extent, we do not accept it."

ABC/AAP

title: Fremantle and Brisbane AFL fans find 'homes away from home' in Melbourne
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Interstate footy fans descending on Melbourne for this weekend's AFL grand final are gravitating towards two pubs serving as unofficial embassies for travelling Fremantle and Brisbane fans.

This weekend is the fifth time two non-Victorian teams are competing in an AFL grand final and interstate fans are already streaming into the city.

An unassuming pub in Melbourne's inner north is gearing up to be a home away from home for Fremantle supporters.

Alistair Carragher bought the Great Northern Hotel in Carlton North in 2009.

The Perth expat said the pub was historically a home for Fremantle and West Coast supporters who moved to Melbourne.

"They'd go play a game of football at the park and then come to the pub after that," he said.

" West Australians in general were a bit neglected in sport and pubs. "

Alistair Carragher says grand final day at the Great Northern has been booked out since May. (ABC News: Ethan White)

Mr Carragher said since 2013, when Fremantle played its first grand final, the popularity of the hotel for local Dockers fans exploded.

"It's great to have somewhere to go, especially being the smaller group in Melbourne, there's not always a place that you can find people," Fremantle cheer squad member Jess Ritchie said.

Dockers fan Nacha Kirilak said it was "nice to have a safe ground to come to with like-minded people who aren't going to yell at you because you're wearing a different colour".

David Cowell, Nacha Kirilak and Jess Ritchie are all members of Fremantle's Melbourne cheer squad. (ABC News: Ethan White)

Along with local supporters, the hotel is expecting to host hundreds of Fremantle fans visiting Melbourne who were unable to get a ticket to the game at the MCG.

"It's a little bit of a community home, somewhere they can see their team," Mr Carragher said.

" Everyone's just super pumped. "

A different story for the Lions

While Dockers supporters in Melbourne needed to commandeer a suburban pub, just a few kilometres to the east, Lions fans had a very different story.

The suburb of Fitzroy is the spiritual home of the Lions, after the Victorian football club amalgamated with the Brisbane Bears 30 years ago, to form the Brisbane Lions.

Scott Villiers, a self-described Lions nuffy, said the team has always felt like the Fitzroy Lions to him.

"It's nostalgic, I actually feel proud to be part of a family, because that's what the Brisbane Lions is," he said.

"The club does an amazing job to preserve the history of both Fitzroy and the Bears."

Brisbane fan Scott Villiers says supporting the Lions is "genetic". (ABC News: Ethan White)

Mr Villiers acknowledged that a new generation of Brisbane fans have emerged since the amalgamation.

"I hope they feel welcome down here, we're an extended family by default," he said.

For the past three grand finals, the Royal Derby Hotel on Brunswick Street has served as the home of the Lions in Fitzroy.

"Thousands upon thousands of bowls of chips, 120 kegs of beer flowing, good vibes and lots of cheering," its venue manager Liam Huxley recalled.

The hotel staff are preparing to do it all again for a fourth consecutive year, while welcoming Queensland fans joining the Fitzroy fraternity.

"Last year, the amount of Bundy [rum] and Great Northern we went through — it's just unbelievable," Mr Huxley said.

Liam Huxley says he's nervous but ready for another premiership. (ABC News: Ethan White)

Victoria to reap the benefits

Both pubs completely booked out tables months ago, with staff expecting hundreds more walk-ins across the long weekend.

RMIT University finance professor Angel Zhong said the grand final weekend could generate up to $75 million in economic activity for the state.

"When interstate fans fly in, stay in hotels and eat in our restaurants, that is genuinely new money entering Victoria," she said.

Events such as the traditional grand final parade draw people into Melbourne's CBD ahead of the game. (ABC News: Richard Sydenham)

Dr Zhong also highlighted the economic strain placed on small business owners, who are required to pay penalty rates on Friday's public holiday in Victoria.

"How it balances out depends on the individual business, whether it opens, how busy it is and whether it can make up the lost day."

Melbourne Airport said more than 114,000 passengers are expected to travel through its terminals on Saturday.

Fans flying from Perth and Brisbane have faced surging flight fares, with return airfares reaching $6,000 ahead of Saturday's game.

While Melburnians may be used to living in the football capital of Australia, this weekend, it's the interstate fans who will be calling the city home.

title: Footballer who died after hitting goalpost remembered for cheeky smile
text:
A 25-year-old footballer who died after hitting a goalpost while being towed by an unregistered quad bike is being remembered as a fierce competitor and much-loved teammate.

Jed Griffin died at the Osborne Football Club's home ground south-west of Wagga Wagga on Sunday afternoon.

A 20-year-old man has been charged with dangerous driving occasioning death, driving in a dangerous manner and negligent driving occasioning death.

He faced a brief hearing in the Wagga Wagga Local Court today. His bail was extended and the case was adjourned until November.

The incident happened one day after Mr Griffin took to the field for the Osborne senior side's game against Henty in the Hume Football Netball League grand final.

Osborne lost the grand final by six points.

Mr Griffin's coach of three years, Myles Aalbers, said Jed was a determined athlete with a cheeky demeanour and a quick-witted sense of humour.

"Every time I would see him, he would just have that cheeky smile … I'll never forget that about Jed," Mr Aalbers said.

" He loved his mates, he loved his outdoor fishing and hunting, and the people close to him. "

Mr Aalbers described Mr Griffin as one of the best footballers he had seen and an all-round great person.

"He was one of the fiercest competitors I've coached with in my time in football," he said.

"Just, with his stature, some of the contest he went into — I was amazed he came out the other end of it with no injuries."

The Osborne Recreation Ground in southern NSW. (ABC News: Jostina Basta )

Griffin committed to Osborne

Mr Aalbers said Mr Griffin's commitment to Osborne was evident in the literal journey he made to play and train, driving past several other clubs between his home and the ground.

"That speaks volumes itself. [It's the] same with his family, Terry, Nicole and Darby. They're a big part of our football club," he said.

He described the Osborne community as a "big family", and said the loss reverberated well beyond the playing group.

"This has obviously impacted a lot of people's lives, and we will aim to get through it together," Mr Aalbers said.

"It is obviously very difficult circumstances. As a playing group we are just trying to rally around each other and stick together as tight as we can.

"We don't know what the steps forward are, but we are just trying to keep the group together and be there for each other."

The club has received support from the wider community, with counselling services offered to players and others affected by Mr Griffin's death.

A floral tribute left at the Osborne Recreation Ground. (ABC News: Jostina Basta )

'Two teams, one league, one united community'

The Hume Football Netball League has been showing its support for the Osborne Football Netball Club, paying tribute to Mr Griffin in online posts.

The Henty Football Netball Club — the team Mr Griffin played his last match against — said it sent love, care and condolences to the 25-year-old's family and loved ones.

It described his death as a "tragic and heartbreaking loss".

"We further extend our arms to the entire Osborne Football Netball Club and all other families impacted by this sad moment in time," the club said.

" Two teams, one league, one united community of people. We are here for you all. "

The Henty Football Netball Club has paid tribute to the footballer online. (Supplied: Facebook.)

The Coreen Daysdale Hopefield Buraja Football Netball Club said it was "deeply saddened by the loss of a really great young man".

"There are simply no words big enough for what you are facing right now," the club said.

"Please know you are not facing it alone. We are right beside you, wrapping our arms around you and sending every bit of love, strength and support we possibly can."

The club said country sporting clubs were "so much more than football and netball".

"They are family. They are where we grow up, where lifelong friendships are formed, where families come together and where we stand beside one another through the very best and the very hardest of times."

The Corowa Rutherglen Football Netball Club, where Mr Griffin played some junior and senior matches, said his's death would leave an enormous hole in the hearts of those who knew him.

"Today, we want to acknowledge the life of Jed — a spirited young man who was loved by so many," the statement read.

"Vale Jed."

Lachie Neale's father says the family is "worried" about the star Lion missing the AFL grand final at the end of a tumultuous year.

Neale copped a one-game suspension for striking Jack Ginnivan during the Lions' stunning preliminary final victory at the MCG on Saturday night, but the club has confirmed it will appeal against the decision.

title: Airport expansion a threat to character of beachside suburb, opponents say
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Community backlash is brewing over a $75 million plan that could transform part of the Sunshine Coast Airport into a resort, residential and retail precinct.

The airport recently submitted an application to state government entity Economic Development Queensland (EDQ) for the 34-hectare site between the runway and homes at Marcoola.

Airport North is listed as a Priority Development Area, which means development applications are accessed by EDQ, bypassing Sunshine Coast Council.

Several community groups and a councillor are urging residents to fight the plan.

Airport North is one of several precincts within the airport site. (Supplied)

Councillor Taylor Bunnag issued a personal statement on Tuesday morning, saying the development "risks destroying our local character".

"This proposal fundamentally risks undoing what makes this part of the Coast special, which generations have fought to protect," the statement said.

A town planning report included in the application seeks approval for a combination of potential uses of the site, including a resort, hotel, short-term accommodation, multiple dwellings, shops, bars, veterinary services, health services, indoor sports and a retirement facility.

Under existing approvals buildings up to 10 storeys high are permitted.

Sekisui development sent back to the drawing board Queensland's Supreme Court rules in favour of a community appeal against the development approval of a controversial beachside development.

Cr Bunnag told the ABC the airport proposal was reminiscent of the Sekisui development planned for Yaroomba, a few suburbs north, which was eventually thrown out by the Supreme Court.

"It is eerily similar in terms of a beachside location, hotels, accommodation," he said.

"I think that this has been the sleeping giant within the community in the sense that, from a council perspective, the airport is no longer under our planning authority."

'Very intense'

The Sunshine Coast Airport Master Plan 2040 states the Airport North precinct would have uses that "may include but are not limited to" logistics, cold storage, warehousing, food and beverage, freight facilities and commercial car parking.

An artist's impression of a hotel planned for the Gateway Precinct near the existing terminal. (Supplied: Sunshine Coast Airport)

Marcoola Community Group president Susie Chapman was involved in consultations for the 2040 plan.

She said the new application was "very intense" for the "low-key" north shore area.

"All our conversations with the master plan was that it wasn't going to be accommodation and it was all going to be internal roadways," Ms Chapman said.

"But this current proposal is certainly nothing of the sort — it's going straight onto David Low Way."

A view of the airport site from David Low Way, which is the main arterial road on the north shore. (Supplied: Taylor Bunnag)

The planning report states the intersection of David Low Way and Green Turtle Place as a "potential site access" point.

"If something happens on the Sunshine Motorway, David Low Way is chock-a-block and held up for hours," she said.

" It really can't take too much more at this stage. "

Development Watch community group member Brian Anker said the plan was a significant "deviation" from the original intent of it being an aviation precinct.

"It's totally out of kilter with the current look and feel of the area," he said.

An artist's impression of the Sunshine Coast Airport's planned Gateway Precinct, located around the existing terminal. (Supplied: Sunshine Coast Airport)

Studies 'still being finalised'

Airport chief executive Chris Mills declined to be interviewed but said in a statement that the airport had submitted the draft plan to EDQ for "initial feedback".

"Key supporting studies, including detailed traffic and flood modelling, are still being finalised in consultation with council and public notification will not commence until this information is complete and available to the community," the statement said.

"We believe it is important that the community has access to the full suite of relevant information when being asked to consider the proposal."

Ms Chapman argued that residents needed to be aware of the plans early so they had time to prepare for the public consultation period.

"People will only get 20 working days so we need to make sure that we're on the front foot," she said.

" This is certainly the greatest call to action that we've had yet. "

title: After a lifetime of achievement, Naomi Watts is just getting started
text:
Advertisement

CultureMoviesFilm Festivals After a lifetime of achievement, Naomi Watts is just getting started Stephanie Bunbury Updated September 23, 2026 — 2:17pm ,first published 12:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Naomi Watts was clearly thrilled to be getting a lifetime achievement award at the San Sebastian Film Festival this week but, after managing to put a stop to the audience’s thunderous applause, she admitted it felt a bit odd. “It’s very strange when you’re in the middle of the journey,” said the one-time star of Australian soap Home and Away. “If anything, I feel I’m just getting started.” Watts, who moved to Hollywood in her early 20s on the strength of her success in Australian films such as Flirting (1991), recalled in her acceptance speech scrabbling for work for 10 years before the late David Lynch cast her as the lead in the seminal film Mulholland Drive. “It wasn’t a smooth ride,” she said. “A lot of people were telling me I wasn’t going to make it. I was too this or not enough of that, not right for this or that: I was always being told what I couldn’t do. But I just kept going; I had this resilience. It was a full 10 years of rejection.” Naomi Watts receives the Donostia lifetime achievement award at the San Sebastian Film Festival. AP Lynch believed in her, she says, before she fully believed in herself. “He saw me and all those wounds from those rejections now appeared as growth. He changed my life.” Every day making that film was fun, she says. “He gave me a different understanding of what it meant to act, to embrace instinct and uncertainty, to not be afraid of the strange or unexplained.” She dedicated her Donostia – the award takes the Basque name for San Sebastian – to him. The success of Mulholland Drive meant that she was seen and then sought out by other top directors including Peter Jackson, Clint Eastwood, Alejandro Gomez Inarritu and David Cronenberg. Spanish director JA Bayona, who directed her Oscar-nominated performance in The Impossible as a mother trapped with her children in the 2004 Thai tsunami. Introducing her to the awards audience, he remembered how she put her trust in him, even though he was new to the game.

Advertisement

Sudden success brought a new episode of discouragement. She was, apparently, almost too old to capitalise on her success. “I was 31 in Mulholland Drive and was told that I’d better get my skates on, because it all finishes at 40. Now here I am, in my late 50s.” Only last week, she pointed out, there were several women over 50 in the Emmy nomination lists. “I do think things have changed. Women are consumers of film and TV and deserve to see their stories reflected,” she said in a press conference for her latest film, The Housewife. “I’m grateful to be part of that shift.” While there are major directors still on her bucket list – in her press conference, she mentioned Paul Thomas Anderson – Watts declared herself still just as excited about working with first-time directors such as Ben Shirinian, who directed her in The Housewife, which is showing in competition in San Sebastian. Set in 1964 and based closely on a real case, the film relates how a cookie-baking, church-going Austrian immigrant was exposed by The New York Times, after a tip-off by Simon Wiesenthal, as a former guard at two concentration camps. Naomi Watts poses during a photocall for her new film The Housewife as it premieres at Spain’s San Sebastian Film Festival. AP “The duality of that woman, living with that secret, was interesting to me as an actor,” she said. At the same time, it was possibly the most difficult role she had ever done, starting with the “shock and awe” she felt reading the script and then researching her abominable crimes. “It was hard to be in that mindset on a daily basis,” she told the press conference. “Anyone here could tell you how conflicted I was after each scene, especially in darker moments.” At a time when hate is on the rise “and it’s a very scary time globally”, she said, cinema and the stories it can tell are more important than ever. Her character Hermine Ryan arrived in the United States at a time when the country supported her belief that it was a place where anyone could start afresh and become what they wanted. Watts herself went to the US, she said, “with hopes and dreams – and way surpassed them”. She has now lived there for decades, discernible in the rolling American “r” sounds that slip in between her Australian vowels and crisp English consonants.

Advertisement

Related Article Vale Elephant Man to Twin Peaks: The six essential David Lynch works Pressed on the state of her adopted nation, she pointed out that she had two American children with actor and former partner Liev Schreiber. “I do love America,” she said in her press conference. “What’s going on today is complicated and nerve-racking, but I have faith things will work out in time.” One of her children identifies as transgender. “I’m proud to be a part of the LGBTQ community,” she said. “Minorities are being attacked right now, and it’s frightful and unacceptable. My heart is with these communities, particularly my family. I’ll do whatever I can to stick up for minorities.” Standing in front of thousands of people – almost all locals – in San Sebastian, however, she recalled her last visit 17 years ago, when The Impossible screened to the home crowd. “The people of San Sebastian are obviously avid film-goers,” she said, “so I’m happy to be here to celebrate with this compelling audience. And I think of the young girl who dreamed of becoming an actor. How is it even possible that I dreamed standing here, three and nearly four decades later? title: Why Dockers fans are putting tape on their team’s guernseys
text:

Fremantle MP Josh Wilson is the latest Dockers fan to jump on a protest against oil and gas giant Woodside’s sponsorship of the club ahead of this weekend’s grand final match. The federal Labor MP, who was taken to the wire by an independent campaign at the last election, was pictured wearing a Dockers guernsey with the Woodside logo covered up in a widely circulated social media post. Federal Labor MP Josh Wilson, centre, pictured with a taped-over Woodside logo on his Dockers guernsey. Tame Impala frontman Kevin Parker (right) also taped over the logo at a concert in Denver last week. And the company’s headquarters in Perth has also been targeted by activists. In a statement, Wilson said the picture in question was a family photo, and “when I wear my Dockers gear I just want to show my support for Freo”. “This week is all about the opportunity to see the Dockers compete on the last Saturday in September, but it’s great that Australia is a place where people have the freedom to express their view and values through a range of creative and peaceful campaigns,” he said.

Advertisement

The move could put Wilson at odds with his Labor colleagues, both federal and state, who have approved a major extension to Woodside’s North West Shelf gas project, and have been open about their support for gas to play a big role as the nation moves away from coal-fired power. It echoes a similar protest by the Dockers’ No.1 ticketholder, Tame Impala frontman Kevin Parker, whose love for his hometown team has been on full display as the band tours the United States. Parker was pictured during a concert at Ball Arena in Denver wearing a Dockers top – again, with the Woodside logo covered over by tape. The protests form part of a growing campaign that has reignited calls for the club to drop Woodside’s sponsorship, following in the footsteps of a similar push in 2023, before the Dockers inked another two-year sponsorship deal the following year. The Get Off My Chest campaign has also sprayed over the Woodside logo on a mural of players Michael Walters and Nat Fyfe that adorns the wall of the Fremantle Markets tourist hotspot.

Advertisement

And, with the help of a projector last week, the activists broadcast another message below the giant “Wharfie Time” banner hanging from Woodside’s Perth headquarters, adding “for a gas tax” to the side of the building. Related Article Fremantle Dockers Tame Impala frontman reignites calls for end to Woodside’s Dockers sponsorship For its part, Woodside has shown no intent to back down from its long-running sponsorship of the team, despite the pressure. “We love our partnership of more than 15 years with the Fremantle Football Club and it’s great to see the success the club is having this year,” a spokesperson said when asked about Wilson’s photo. “We’re looking forward to continuing our work together.”

Advertisement

Still, if fans flocking to the port city on Saturday are desperate for a reprieve from the oil and gas giant’s advertising, they may find solace in the (mostly) environmentally conscious local council’s policies. The City of Fremantle adopted a policy last year that “does not support advertising of or by companies involved in the production or supply of fossil fuels owned or managed by the City”. “The City of Fremantle does not support advertising which specifically promotes fossil fuels on property owned or managed by the City,” the policy states. There is a caveat that fossil fuel ads may be displayed during or to promote an event as part of a sponsorship agreement, but it must not be displayed more than 48 before the event, and must be removed within 48 hours of the event’s conclusion. It’s worth noting that Fremantle Oval, in the heart of the CBD, where thousands of Dockers fans will converge on Saturday, is owned by the local council.

Critical Resources has planted its flag in South America after striking a savvy deal for the exclusive right to acquire a 90 per cent interest in the Gonini gold project in Suriname. The move gives the company a rare first-mover advantage for an ASX-listed junior, establishing a foothold in the highly prospective Guiana Shield gold province. And the market appeared to greet the news with a loud cheer, pushing the company’s share price as much as 29 per cent higher to 0.9 of a cent in early trade, on the biggest turnover in more than three months. Excavator-assisted artisanal workings at the Gonini gold project in Suriname, South America pictured in 2020. A geological province Critical Resources says is analogous to West Africa’s prolific Birimian gold belts. The 164-square-kilometre project comprises two granted exploitation rights in the historic Sara Creek gold district, a region with a 150-year history of artisanal and small-scale mining but, notably, no record of modern, systematic exploration. Under the terms of the heavily bank-ended deal, Critical will pay a US$50,000 (A$70,300) signing fee, followed by a completion payment of US$200,000 (A$281,250) in cash and 10 million Critical Resources shares. A series of deferred cash payments totalling US$1.75 (A$2.46) million are payable over the subsequent four years to the vendor, N.V. Gonini Mining Company.

‘This is a gold province with major mines, major discoveries and growing strategic investment.’ Critical Resources managing director Tim Wither Critical has also committed to a minimum exploration expenditure of US$2.5 (A$3.52) million over five years. The vendor will retain a 10 per cent free-carried interest to a decision to mine, in addition to a 2 per cent net smelter return royalty that the company can buy back. The Gonini project sits within the Marowijne greenstone belt, which is proven elephant country. The project lies just 66 kilometres from Newmont’s massive 5.1-million-ounce Merian mine and 88km from Zijin Mining’s 5.6-million-ounce Rosebel operation. The company is quick to point out that mineralisation at those mines is not necessarily indicative of what it might find at Gonini, but the address is undeniably first-class. Critical says the project area straddles the contact between the Paramaka greenstone belt and a tonalite-granodiorite intrusive, a geological setting associated with orogenic gold mineralisation elsewhere in the region. Notably, since the Gonini project comes with granted exploitation rights, the company will have immediate access for exploration, mining, processing and the sale of minerals, avoiding the lengthy processes often required to convert an exploration permit into a mining right.

Critical Resources managing director Tim Wither said: “We believe Gonini gives Critical Resources a rare first-mover position on the ASX: a large, granted gold tenure package in Suriname at a time when global mining capital is increasingly recognising the discovery potential of the Guiana Shield. This is a gold province with major mines, major discoveries and growing strategic investment - but still a fraction of the modern exploration maturity seen elsewhere along the Guiana Shield greenstone belt.” Critical’s entry into Suriname comes at a time when the region is heating up, with major international mining companies and strategic investors increasingly recognising its gold discovery potential. The Guiana Shield, which also covers neighbouring Guyana and French Guiana, is the geological counterpart to West Africa’s famously rich Birimian Greenstone Belt, which has so far coughed up a staggering 500 million ounces of gold. While Critical may be one of the first on the ASX to offer exposure to the region, it is, nevertheless, following a trail blazed by its North American-listed peers. Canadian-listed explorers such as Founders Metals, Miata Metals and Greenheart Gold have all attracted significant strategic capital from mining giants including Gold Fields and La Mancha after unearthing high-grade gold on Surinamese ground. Elsewhere, the company continues to roll out its Mavis Lake lithium project in Canada, home to an 8Mt resource at 1.07 per cent lithium oxide. It also holds an option over solid-state battery-technology intellectual property and has licensed thermal management tech targeting AI high-density electronics data centres. Additionally, Critical holds the Halls Peak base metals project in New South Wales featuring an inferred resource of 840,000 tonnes at 3.7 per cent zinc, 1.5 per cent lead and 0.44 per cent copper. At the same time, it is advancing a growing portfolio of gold, antimony and tungsten prospects across a 1694-square-kilometre ground package in New Zealand.

Gonini features a history of artisanal workings that have exposed weathered bedrock, giving Critical a ready-made starting point for exploration. The company plans to get boots on the ground after the deal is finalised, which is slated within the next 90 days. Its first field campaign is expected to channel-sample exposed pit walls, saprolite and weathered bedrock before rolling into geochemistry, trenching and targeted geophysics. Initial soil lines are planned across the interpreted greenstone-batholith contact, with auger sampling to help peer beneath the deep tropical weathering profile. With a swag of ASX-listed companies now trying to get a foothold in West Africa’s Birimian Shield, it is perhaps more than curious that its geological cousin in South America has been largely overlooked. Now, with a solid ground position, advanced tenure and a clear playbook in a region that is starting to deliver for others, Critical Resources has given itself every chance to change that story. title: ‘So flawed’: Satterley loses bid to build 1000-lot housing estate in Perth bushfire zone
text:
Advertisement

Updated PoliticsWAPlanning and development ‘So flawed’: Satterley loses bid to build 1000-lot housing estate in Perth bushfire zone Hamish Hastie September 23, 2026 — 12:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Developer Nigel Satterley’s long-held dream to build a 1001-lot town site in Perth’s hills has been dealt a fatal blow with the State Administrative Tribunal rejecting his eponymous company’s structure plan for the site. While noting there was a housing crisis, the tribunal rejected Satterley Group’s structure plan for the 535-hectare bush site that was to house up to 2800 people, describing it as flawed and unable to proceed even with modification. Satterley Property Group has been fighting to build its North Stoneville development in the Perth Hills for decades. Jamie Brown/WAtoday The brutal decision is a huge win for opponents of the plan, the Save Perth Hills group, which has been fighting urbanisation of the area for nearly four decades. Save Perth Hills spokeswoman Debra Bishop was elated.

Advertisement

“After 35 years, Save Perth Hills and the community has saved Perth Hills. We have won. We have beaten a plan that was putting profit before people,” she told ABC Perth. Bishop called on the Anglican Church, who own the land, to abandon its plans for North Stoneville in favour of rural lots. “Rezone your land to rural, five to 10 acres and bigger. It’s safer in bushfires, environmentally more sensitive, and you will get the support of the local community,” she said. The tribunal upheld the Western Australian Planning Commission’s 2020 rejection of the North Stoneville structure plan, agreeing the risks posed to lives by such a massive influx in population in such a bushfire prone area was unacceptable. The Tribunal said the structure plan did not adhere with state bushfire planning policy, which prioritised the preservation of life and the strict management of bushfire impacts in planning.

Advertisement

“Section 2 of SPP 3.7 provides that the preservation of life and the management of bushfire impact are ‘paramount’ and, as we have been at pains to reiterate, SPP 3.7 and the guidelines require the management of bushfire risk, where it cannot be avoided altogether, to an acceptable level,” it said in its decision. “We find that the structure plan does not demonstrate that that can be done on the site. “Indeed, in our view the structure plan proceeds on the basis of such basic flaws that it cannot be ‘saved’ by the making of modifications. “Our finding is that the structure plan put before us and relied upon by Satterley is so flawed as to warrant a refusal to approve it.” A spokeswoman for Satterley Group said the company was disappointed with the decision but would need to review the judgment.

Advertisement

“Given the significance of the decision and the detailed matters considered through the proceedings we will take the necessary time to carefully review the Tribunal’s reasons in full and consider the implications for the site,” she said. A spokeswoman for the Anglican Diocese of Perth thanked the SAT and said the church would take some time to reflect and take advice on the most appropriate next steps. Perth property developer Nigel Satterley has been fighting for years to build the North Stoneville development. Trevor Collens During the SAT hearings, lawyers for Satterley argued modelling it had done around traffic and human behaviour proved the development could go ahead safely. However, the company conceded its dream to establish the townsite would not be realised until a major upgrade of Toodyay Road is complete – which may not happen until the 2040s.

Advertisement

The company argued that, with mooted Main Roads upgrades to nearby Seaborne Street and Great Eastern Highway, they could still safely pursue between 350 and 400 lots at the site until EastLink was complete. WAPC lawyers also revealed Satterley had offered to only build 135 lots at the site until road improvements were complete. The tribunal rejected the company’s modelling and its arguments around human behaviour during a bushfire. “The evidence provides a strong basis for a finding that bushfire evacuations are, generally speaking, ‘chaotic and confusing’ and that people, including those that have prepared well for the eventuality, make decisions that might be said to appear to be irrational,” it said. The tribunal, however, flagged that its decision did not mean the area was not suitable for urban development.

Advertisement

“What decisions others make as to the future of the site is a matter for them, informed by the facts and circumstances and, indeed, any future proposed structure plan, of the time,” it said. Urbanisation of North Stoneville has been ferociously rejected by the surrounding community since it was first floated in 1991. It has also been rejected by the Shire of Mundaring council, the Department of Fire and Emergency Services, in more than 4000 public submissions, and twice by WA’s highest planning authority since 2020. The community opposition revolves around the loss of native bushland and fire risk. The WAPC rejected the most recent North Stoneville structure plan in December 2023 because of the bushfire risk. Tribunal Judge Henry Jackson has been mulling a decision since public hearings concluded late last year.

title: The numbers raising new questions about Australia's future wealth
text:
in brief Treasury data suggests lower migration barely impacts individual Australian wealth.

Experts warn smaller migrant numbers increase fiscal burdens for retirees.

Australian living standards would not collapse if population growth targets are not met in the future, Treasury forecasts predict, with households revealed to be just a few hundred dollars worse off even with a drastically different size.

The difference between a high migration and a low migration scenario in the next 40 years, may only pan out to affect GDP per capita by about $400, the figures suggest.

However, experts caution that governments will need to make "tough decisions" around funding if fewer migrants were to arrive in the country, as a shrinking tax base would have to support a growing dependent population of retirees.

Some of the government's political opponents have cited the results of the Intergenerational Report (IGR) to claim that migration levels need to be cut further than current government projections.

Published by the federal government every three years since 2002, the IGR outlines Australia's economic and budgetary outlook over the next 40 years.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The forecasts in the reports are predictions, some of which have fallen far off the mark, such as the first report projecting that Australia's population would reach 25 million in 2042 — a milestone reached 24 years earlier in 2018.

Its release comes amid an ongoing public debate over optimal net overseas migration figures, which the Coalition and One Nation parties argue should be reduced.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers has defended the government's forecast that annual migration to Australia will drop to 225,000 people by 2028.

He said migration is "a force for good in our economy and in our society".

"We will continue to make the case for getting that net overseas migration down in the most responsible way, that balances all of the key considerations in our economy and in local communities," Chalmers told the ABC's 7.30 program on Monday.

While fewer people in the country may alleviate some structural pressures on housing, infrastructure, and public services, Dr Liz Allen, senior lecturer in demography at the Australian National University, told SBS News that migration cannot be separated from its broader impacts on society.

"There's no optimal population size. That's just the reality," she said. "We need to look at what's going on underneath."

What the data tells us

Data in the IGR, released on Monday, shows that under a low migration scenario of 185,000 annually, GDP per capita would shrink by just $400 in 2066, compared with the baseline assumption of 235,000.

Under a higher migration scenario of 285,000, gross national income per capita (GNI) would be just $100 more, despite adding some 2 million people over the 40-year projection period.

GDP per capita refers to a country's total economic output, divided by population. GNI refers to total earnings by a country's people and businesses.

The country's population would climb by roughly 5.5 to 6 million, from around 36 million under a low-migration scenario, to around 42 million in a high-migration scenario by 2066. However Australians would only be up by $500 annually.

Allen said that while individual slices might remain virtually identical, the size of the cake as a whole would be smaller.

"With a shrinking relative working-age population, living standards could go backwards as the government needs to do more with less money," she said.

The fiscal drag of ageing

While per capita GDP and GNI remain virtually identical, national GDP growth drops from 1.6 to 1.3 per cent with fewer migrants as the projections reveal the country would face substantial challenges if migration numbers do not match the forecasts.

Under the low-migration scenario, gross debt as a percentage of GDP would rise by 4.8 per cent while total payments on aged care, the NDIS, healthcare, and other spending would increase by 0.6 per cent.

The old-age dependency ratio — the number of people aged 65 or over for every 100 workers — is projected to rise from 27.4 to 40.2. With fewer migrants, that burden climbs to 43, but with more, it drops to 37.8.

Erin-Lea Brown, economic prosperity deputy program director at the Grattan Institute, said higher migration would help to alleviate issues of an ageing population.

"You have this softening of the ageing population effect," she said. "Our population would still absolutely age over that time period, and it would be a major structural trend in our economy, but it would be to a lesser degree."

Productivity over population

The IGR finds that changes in productivity would be far more significant to national wealth.

The Treasury's baseline productivity is assumed to be 1.2 per cent of GDP, but it also modelled it to be as low as 0.8 or as high as 1.6.

Under a high-productivity scenario, GNI per capita surges from $149,500 to $172,000 in 2066, and gross debt falls from 27.4 per cent of GDP to just 2.4 per cent of GDP.

Labour productivity growth — the ability to "do more with less" — has driven growth in real GDP per person over the past 40 years, Brown said.

As population growth slows and the boost to participation driven by women entering the workforce over the past 40 years levels out, it will become "even more important for labour productivity to do the heavy lifting", Brown said, to "ensure that we continue to have economic growth into the future".

Paying for the future

Australia is far from the only country with a fertility rate — the number of babies born to each woman — below the 2.1 needed to keep the population stable.

More than half of countries have a birth rate below the replacement level, while countries such as Italy, South Korea, China, and Japan have rapidly shrinking populations.

Given that government fiscal policy relies largely on taxing its working population, Allen said a reconsideration of taxation is needed given the long-term demographic shifts Australia is facing.

On Monday, Chalmers ruled out making changes to GST while also rejecting proposals to implement an inheritance tax.

Allen, however, said tax reform can come from elsewhere by "taxing corporates, taxing other entities, and taxing the non-renewable products of the earth from Australia".

"Unless we see some major change to the way that taxation and government funding is conducted in this place, future governments are going to have to make tough decisions."

Intergenerational reports, experts note, are useful because they force governments to "lift their eyes" from the next election to think about long-term planning. Rather than trying to predict the future, they try to capture the impact of present policies in 40 years time if nothing changes.

"In a way, a successful IGR may actually be one whose forecasts never eventuate because it exposed an unsustainable path and forced a change of some kind," Brown said.

Allen added that politicians should not be using the report to "stoke fear" but to rally together to work on the "scary" problems of the future.

"We fix these things by making the future more hopeful, so that folks have greater certainty, and tomorrow looks promising."
