title: As world leaders arrive in the US, there's one question they want answered
text:
In brief World leaders have signed a statement on AI regulation ahead of a leaders' meeting at the UN General Assembly this week.

Anthony Albanese has been praised as a "trailblazer" for Australia's under-16 social media ban.

In the hyper-colour, futuristic crush of New York City's Times Square, a man who calls himself "Scientific" reflects on the march of artificial intelligence (AI).

He told SBS News the realities of AI have already arrived, with power both awesome and deeply confronting.

"You got to adapt with it. If you don’t adapt, in 10 years we are going to become extinct," he said.

Scientific is a musician. He wants more regulation of the technology companies.

"It's going left and right with this artificial intelligence … right now it’s acting like it's human.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"If it has too much freedom over creativity, and gets the credit, what do they need us for?"

He's not alone. Everyone we spoke to in Manhattan's billboard-encrusted tourist magnet expressed concern about where the technology is leading humanity.

Another man urged some regulation be fast-tracked to ensure that AI agents don't decide humans are doing dangerous things and "get rid of them".

That's despite most people we spoke to also conceding they rely on ChatGPT and other AI assistants to help streamline their work and home lives.

Scientific, a musician, wants greater regulation over big tech companies pushing AI. Source: SBS News / Anna Henderson

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has played a "central role" in crafting a statement alongside a broad coalition of international leaders, calling for control of frontier artificial intelligence models.

That statement was publicly released on Tuesday ahead of the United Nations General Assembly leaders' week.

Signatories represent Norway, Finland, Bahrain, Canada, Denmark, Estonia, Germany, Iceland, Ireland, Kazakhstan, Kenya, Latvia, Moldova, the Netherlands, Singapore, Spain, South Africa, Türkiye and the United Arab Emirates

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has also signed up, and in a meeting with Albanese referred to him as a "trailblazer" in reference to Australia's social media laws.

READ MORE We came to meet Tim Cook, but left with just a few photos

The leaders of other nations are being encouraged to add heft to the message, which acknowledges AI's power to improve people's lives but sounds the alarm about safety risks if the technology is mismanaged.

"Leading scientists and executives are warning that the pace of development could outpace our ability to manage emerging risks," the statement said.

"To realise AI's potential, industry, governments and society must act now. We must address these risks and strengthen oversight — without widening the gap between countries in access to the benefits of AI."

"AI must remain under human direction, oversight and control. It must be developed and used in line with international law."

It commends companies that have transparent safety controls and endorses common standards that encourage the sharing of safety incidents.

The statement proposes an international institution to set standards and provide oversight to "convene states when capability thresholds are crossed".

Albanese wants to build on the international reputation he's achieved through the under-16s social media ban by helping shape how the world approaches the AI challenge.

"If it's going to be successful, then we need to make sure that humans are at the centre of everything that occurs," Albanese said.

In some ways, the world leaders who address the UN this week are a sideshow. The real draw is the main AI negotiations set to take place between the United States and Chinese presidents at the White House later this week.

But this statement is intended to lobby US President Donald Trump to consider further protections. So far, he's indicated that’s not his preference.

"We hope for a positive meeting," Albanese said.

"Other nations are putting forward their national interest.

"Australians do want to know that artificial intelligence won't be in control of us."

Whether the tech industry would comply with the demands of UN member states is unclear.

Sam Altman, CEO of ChatGPT developer OpenAI, is expected to address an open session of the UN Security Council this week.

Many people SBS News spoke to in Manhattan's billboard-encrusted Times Square expressed concern about where AI is leading humanity. Source: SBS News / Anna Henderson

Back in Times Square, a man in a gorilla costume poses for photos, while smart glasses flash up on one of the hundreds of advertising screens behind him.

The companies advancing AI know they are the giant gorillas in this AI race.

US television networks staged an extraordinary revolt Monday when they effectively boycotted coverage of President Donald Trump in protest at his decision to ban three leading outlets from the White House.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico also went to court after Trump on Saturday ordered them to be barred, as the 80-year-old Republican stepped up his years-long assault on the US media.

As a result of the row, Trump's opening of his cherished new White House helipad and his trip to the United Nations General Assembly were proceeding without live television coverage.

In a rare move, US broadcasters ABC, CBS, NBC, Fox News, and CNN said on Tuesday that they were halting "pool" coverage of the White House — where a broadcaster films on behalf of all television outlets for the day — in solidarity with CNN.

CNN had been scheduled to serve on Tuesday as the White House TV pool.

"The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting," ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC said in a statement.

The result is an almost unprecedented test of wills between the Trump administration and the press, in a critical week during which Chinese President Xi Jinping is visiting the White House.

Media 'like cancer'

There will be no live TV of Trump's meetings with foreign leaders at the UN in New York, an annual forum that is closely watched around the world.

Meanwhile, the ribbon-cutting ceremony for the giant granite helipad on the South Lawn was only streamed on the White House's website — and Trump's comments were completely inaudible.

Several photo news organisations working at the White House decided to delay the release of photographs of Trump at the helipad in solidarity with the three banned media organisations.

Trump was unrepentant, branding the media a "cancer" and a threat to national security.

"The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish," Trump said on his Truth Social network.

"It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America."

Vice President JD Vance — a former CNN commentator before his move into politics — accused the outlets of disseminating "left-wing propaganda."

"They can still report. They still have the access to free speech. They're just not going to get an office in the White House anymore," he told reporters.

Trump's ban, however, went further than simply revoking office space from the outlets.

Journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were denied any access to the White House grounds on Saturday and had their passes confiscated.

In their lawsuit, the three organisations asked for a temporary restraining order against the ban on the grounds that it violates the First Amendment of the US Constitution, which upholds the right to a free press.

"This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles," the organisations said in a court filing.

A US district judge set a hearing on the complaint for Wednesday.

Press passes confiscated

Trump's sudden announcement of the ban on Saturday stunned the media — and reportedly many in his own administration.

The president has not detailed what prompted the ban, but said in response to a question from a reporter from the Agence France-Presse news agency in the Oval Office on Friday that it was "really just cumulative stories over the last two years."

Trump warned on Saturday that other outlets could face a similar fate, without saying which.

The billionaire former reality TV star has long attacked media outlets that have aired critical coverage of his campaigns and administrations, repeatedly blasting the press as the "enemy of the people."

But the ban comes at a time when his approval ratings are at record lows, his Republican Party risks losing control of Congress in November's midterm elections, and the Iran war drags on with no end in sight.

title: Would giving Australians $75,000 change the country's future?
text:
in brief Australia faces a choice between higher immigration or having more babies to fix an ageing workforce and shrinking tax base.

Experts say migration is the most effective strategy to staff essential sectors like aged care long term.

Australia will need to boost its population to support the elderly and the economy in the long term, experts warn, after the government's latest Intergenerational Report (IGR) found that people are expected to live longer and have fewer children.

The report landed as politicians float the idea of bringing back the Howard-era baby bonus and argue over the need to reduce migration.

Independent MP Bob Katter has recently suggested an up-front cash payment of $75,000 per child would reverse the declining birth rate, which is now expected to fall to just 1.34 children per woman by 2065.

The argument was dismissed by Treasurer Jim Chalmers and Nationals leader Matt Canavan, who said on Monday that family support policy should be more than just "here's some cash".

However, Australia does face challenging demographic questions, with experts saying the choice will come down to more migrants or more babies.

"We will have a large pool of elderly people that we have to support," Dr Pelin Akyol, research manager at the economic think tank The e61 Institute, told SBS News.

"If we have a smaller pool of people working, then it will be a big fiscal problem in this country — and in every country."

Global and domestic surveys show that most people want to have more children than they end up having, owing to cultural, social, and economic constraints which are difficult to address.

"With AI and everything else going on right now, it is hard to know what will happen," Akyol said. "But what we know at this point is that it's going to affect the economy in a bad way".

The fertility illusion

While the IGR highlights a collapsing birth rate, demographers caution that official metrics paint a distorted picture of Australian family choices.

Peter McDonald, emeritus professor of demography at the Australian National University, told SBS News that the country's reliance on international students and temporary visa holders skewed the headline Total Fertility Rate (TFR).

Temporary migrants are often young adults aged 20 to 35 who are in higher education or the early stages of their career. While they are counted as potential mothers, they "hardly have any births," McDonald said, which drives the TFR down.

Previous Intergenerational Reports have predicted that Australia would have a higher fertility rate.

"That's one of the central reasons why Australia's fertility rate has been falling because the temporary population's been rising," he said.

The birth rate for women born in Australia is around 1.64, higher than the Australian Bureau of Statistics headline fertility rate of 1.48. While this is still below the replacement rate of 2.1, Akyol said the immigration influence on TFR is different in Australia than in other comparable nations.

"In Germany, migrants have higher fertility rate than natives," she said. "But in Australia, it is the opposite".

READ MORE Cheryll tried to get pregnant for years. One thing sealed her decision to stop

McDonald also warns against placing too much faith in the long-term projections of the IGR — which assumes net overseas migration will remain flat at 235,000 annually for the next four decades — and that immigration and total births can't be viewed separately as they are "not independent of each other".

"If you can tell me what the birth rate is going to be in 10 years, you're a better man than me," he said. "But if you can tell me what it is in 40 years, then you're a miracle worker."

Is a baby bonus the answer?

Katter's proposed return to former treasurer Peter Costello's cash payment for each newborn child would cost upwards of an estimated $22.5 billion a year for the present 300,000 babies born each year in Australia.

Akyol's research into the 2004 policy indicates that cash incentives do increase the fertility rate, but the effect is "not huge" and, given how different the world is today, "it is not guaranteed we will see a similar effect".

While a $75,000 payment is "huge" compared to the $3,000 of the original policy and "might have an effect", Akyol doubted this was the best use of money when other factors like support benefits also play a key role in family decisions.

Independent Queensland federal MP Bob Katter has said a $75,000 payment per baby would reverse Australia's declining birth rate — experts disagree. Source: AAP

McDonald said Australia's tax system has become too narrowly focused on early childcare, making raising older children harder for working families.

"Today, about 58 per cent of families get no family allowance for their children," he said. "It's not just about very young children... supporting families with children is also about supporting older children, and we've gone a long, long way away from doing that."

A median worker claiming both employer and state parental leave would already receive around $48,700 before tax, something McDonald said disadvantages those without full-time employment. Instead of re-introducing lump-sum payments, he calls for a broader review of child equity.

"I think there's a need for an inquiry into the system of child support payments, to deal with two issues: one is the inequity of the system for very young children, and two, the lack of support for older children," he said.

"Children are a social good.... so I think there is justification for supporting families with children; it's called horizontal equity."

"Horizontal equity used to be quite a big thing back in the 1980s ... I think it needs to be revisited."

A national trade-off

To offset a declining taxpayer base, the IGR highlights increasing older workforce participation and leveraging artificial intelligence to automate labour gaps.

However, McDonald questioned the feasibility of expecting Australians to work deeper into their 60s and 70s.

"A lot of people, particularly those who work in physically demanding jobs, do not want to work beyond pension age. They've had enough," he said.

"AI is going to make a big difference to future labour force needs, but AI is not going to wipe the bottoms of people in aged care."

Akyol said current debates around migration could soon flip as birth rates drop across the globe, including in key migrant origin countries such as China and India. With a shrinking global talent pool, nations could shift from seeking to restrict migration to actively competing for skilled workers.

"In the long run, there might really be a competition for getting the best migrants," Akyol said. "Because in all developed countries, fertility rate has been decreasing... and it seems like there is no hope that it will just turn back and increase again."

"There is no easy solution here. There is a trade-off with every kind of policy."

Relying on immigration is the most direct mechanism to address workforce shortages in sectors like aged care, which are already under strain, McDonald said — something he said the government has failed to communicate in its messaging.

"The IGR shows the advantage of a higher level of migration for the federal government's bottom line," McDonald said. "Migrants make our prospects of dealing with a future aged population much better."

title: 'Rules need to be upheld': The powerful UN privilege Australia wants to rein in
text:
Australia would push to reform the United Nations if given a seat on its Security Council, Foreign Minister Penny Wong has said, as she joined Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in New York for the United Nations General Assembly.

Speaking with SBS News, Wong said Russia's use of veto powers to exempt itself from repercussions during its invasion of Ukraine was an example of where Australia would seek reform.

"We've had a longstanding position as a country of reform of the veto, and we know it's been misused previously," Wong told SBS News on Monday.

"What happened in relation to Russia's invasion of Ukraine was that a permanent member of the Security Council used its veto to prevent any action being taken for its own breach of the charter. That was an example where we would like reform."

Fifteen countries sit on the Security Council, and its five permanent members — China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States — have the right to veto any resolution or decision.

In 2022, Russia vetoed a Security Council resolution that described its attempts to unlawfully annex four regions of Ukraine as “a threat to international peace and security”, demanding Russia “immediately, completely and unconditionally withdraw all of its military forces” from Ukrainian territory. Ten of fifteen members had voted in favour of the resolution, while four abstained.

Wong said that Australia was "for reform", but that Australians were "very practical people".

"We recognise rules need to be upheld; the UN needs to be reformed.

"We want to make sure, where it really matters, that we continue to be part of setting the direction about that reform."

Wong has backed Albanese's bid for a seat on the council, which Australia has not held since 2014. Asked whether the veto powers in their current state rendered the campaign redundant, Wong stood by the pursuit.

"We might be distant from New York, but we are not distant from the rest of the world, and the world does have an effect on what happens in our economy, in our lives.

"So what I would say is we want to be able to advocate for Australia's interests in every forum that matters, and the UN Security Council matters."

International law under 'pressure'

International law is under a "great deal of pressure", Wong said, but the best response would be for countries to "come together" and advocate for the observance of international law.

"You've got two options, don't you? You can throw your hands up and say, 'I give up'. Or you can say, 'This actually matters to many countries.'

"We're not a superpower, but we're a country with substance and power to work with others to try and ensure that we hold onto the rules that matter."

Asked whether Australia could hold the United States to account over accusations around the war in Iran, as well as its actions in Venezuela, Wong said it was a task for the international community to work out the rules that "we really want to hold on to, that matter to us".

"I think trading arrangements matter to us. They certainly matter to Australia, and we've been very clear about our difference with the Trump administration."

But Australia does not intend to join its like-minded international partners in broader sanctions on Israeli settlements on the West Bank, Wong said, referring to "targeted sanctions" announced earlier this month as the UK banned trade in the occupied territories, and nine European countries said they were considering the same.

"I've announced already that we would engage in targeted sanctions," Wong said, noting that no country that had announced it would engage in the sanctions on a blanket basis had yet implemented them.

"And we certainly will be working with them as they do that to understand how they intend to deal with that," she said, and added that she has a "very clear intention" of engaging in more action against settlements, "which are an obstacle to peace", and "engaging in behaviour which makes two states less likely" in the case of the E-1 settlement, a contentious development plan for a 12-square-kilometre corridor in the West Bank.

"We'll continue to work closely with our like-minded countries just as we did a year ago, when, with others, we recognised the state of Palestine, which was part of the precursor to the peace plan, which we want to see implemented."

title: Does Australia's favourite travel destination hold the secret to a longer life?
text:
In brief Ageing populations are increasing worldwide, including in Australia.

Japan has had a dwindling birth rate and ageing population for decades.

This article contains a reference to suicide.

Long famous for the longevity of its citizens, Japan surpassed a record 100,000 people aged 100 or older this year.

According to the country's health, labour and welfare ministry, Japan's number of centenarians increased for the 56th consecutive year to 107,677 — 88 per cent of whom were women.

Ageing populations are increasing worldwide, including in Australia, where life expectancy, already the third-highest in the world behind Monaco and Japan, is expected to climb over the next 40 years.

According to the Australian government's latest Intergenerational Report, released on Monday, Australia's ageing population is expected to transform the economy.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

As we look to a future with an older population and a longer life expectancy, what lessons can Australia take from Japan?

Henry Brodaty, Scientia professor of ageing and mental health at the University of New South Wales, said there were some obvious differences between Japan and Australia, notably the former's healthier lifestyle: Japanese people largely eat fewer high-fat and ultra-processed foods.

"They eat a lot of fish, which has been associated with a better diet and a lower risk of dementia," Brodaty told SBS News.

He said that social isolation and alcohol intake, both risk factors for dementia, were lower in Japan than in Australia, though Japan had high rates of high blood pressure and vascular disease. Stress levels were also much higher than Australia's.

"In fact, our suicide rate is about 12 to 100,000," Brodaty said. "And theirs is about 16 to 100,000."

Urban supports for longevity

Professor Marco Amati from RMIT University's Centre for Urban Research said Japan has elderly care baked into its urban planning.

"One of the biggest challenges for Australia is to do with aged care facilities, which have many issues; notably, there was a royal commission into that," he told SBS News.

Amati said Japan was good at providing end-of-life care for the elderly, with a clear commitment to providing social housing, public transport, and amenities to a high enough standard as to allow people to "age in place". Amati described this as the "Holy Grail", the "most dignified way to age".

"Everybody would prefer to remain at home, surrounded by your community, age in place, and pass away in a familiar environment," he said.

"If you have a situation where people own their own home, and they have to sell their house to go into aged care, that can be very traumatic."

By contrast, in Japan, housing communities are set up to allow ageing in place, including in rental accommodation or in public housing, and for people with early-onset dementia.

READ MORE Aged care giant refunds $200,000 to residents over disputed living fees

In such places, technological advancements have enabled the monitoring of elderly residents in non-obtrusive ways, ensuring that any end-of-life incidents do not go unnoticed — a common issue for elderly people with few surviving relatives.

Amati said that while similar housing approaches may not be achievable in Australia, they were still useful to know about.

"In Australia it's a whole different mix," he said. "But having that kind of a commitment or even knowing that it exists is useful to know."

Australia's biggest threat to long life

The biggest threat to long life in Australia is dementia, which in 2024 overtook cancer and heart disease to become Australia's biggest killer nationally.

Brodaty quoted recent figures from a US study published in the journal Nature: for people aged 55, the lifetime risk of dementia was 42 per cent.

"It's a scary statistic," Brodaty said.

READ MORE Want to reduce your dementia risk? Lifestyle changes are only part of the picture

The earlier people embrace brain health, the higher their chances of living longer. Importantly, Brodaty says, their chances of maintaining good lifetime cognition were higher, too.

"Eating a diet that's rich in vegetables, legumes, extra virgin olive oil, fish, lesser amounts of red meat and sweets, lesser amounts of processed food, watching their blood pressure and getting it checked and treated if it's high," were the best practices, Brodaty said.

Keeping socially connected and having purpose in life were also important. People who live longer "have something that drives them to live and feel valued".

Importantly, Brodaty said there were many simple ways to reduce your chances of getting dementia by almost half.

"We cannot smoke; we can avoid head injury if we can, avoid or treat diabetes. We know that people who have more exposure to green spaces and blue spaces also have a lower rate of dementia," Brodaty said.

"Eating well, remaining socially connected, keeping our brains active, using our brains, being physically active. Exercise is one of the best things we can do for our health in multiple ways."

Living longer, but at what cost?

But the comparison between Australia and Japan can only go so far, Brodaty said.

"We have to consider the demography of the two countries. Australia has 26,270,000 people. Japan has over 100,000,000 people."

Japan's long-lived, ageing population underscores a severe demographic crisis. It's part of the reason the number of centenarians seems "distorted", Brodaty said.

Japan has had a dwindling birth rate and ageing population for decades.

"This is really quite a crisis for Japan economically, because the number of people of working age, proportionately, is decreasing, and the number of people of working age who can look after older people is shrinking."

In Japan, there are roughly two working-age people for every elderly person aged 65 or older.

"Imagine that if we have only one person of working age to help support every older person," Brodaty asked. "How could we possibly arrange our society to deal with that?"

Brodaty said that while this would be an increasing crisis, there was a way to avert it.

"That is to try to help people live their lifespan healthily," he said. "So we talk about healthspan and lifespan, and that gap is what we're trying to narrow."

title: German chancellor declares AfD state election win 'a disaster'
text:
In brief The far-right AfD secured its latest state-level election win in eastern Germany.

The result puts fresh pressure on German Chancellor Friedrich Merz as his party suffers a historic setback.

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has won state elections in north-east Germany, delivering the worst result for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative party since 1949.

"It's a disaster," Merz said after exit polls were published on Monday, but signalled he would fight on as chancellor and continue his reform agenda, despite speculation that a bad result could prompt him to resign.

The AfD was set to win 37 per cent in the state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, ahead of the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) on 35.5 per cent and far in front of Merz’s conservatives, who got 5.5 per cent and barely crossed the threshold to enter the state parliament, according to exit polls on ARD public television.

Sunday's result looks set to deliver another first-place finish at the state level in a month for the AfD party, which tops national opinion polls but has been kept out of power by the other main parties' refusal to work with it.

In another election in the capital, Berlin, which also took place on Sunday, the far-left Die Linke party was at 24.5 per cent, while Merz's conservatives were at 20 per cent.

The AfD also gained in strength in the liberal city, hitting 16 per cent. It is the first time the Linke topped polls in the state, where it wants to nationalise housing from corporate landlords and cap rents.

The elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a largely rural state in the formerly communist east, and in the capital, Berlin, follow the 6 September election in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD came close to the rare feat of winning an absolute majority.

Elections in the two states would not usually draw much interest outside Germany, but the AfD's success in Saxony-Anhalt, which it sees as the first step towards winning federal elections due in 2029, has sent shock waves through Europe.

In just over a decade, the party, which wants to take tough action to deport foreigners with no right to stay in Germany, restore energy ties with Russia, and quit the euro, has transformed itself from a fringe eurosceptic movement into the country's most popular party.

The exit polls underscore the advances the AfD has made in recent years and raise fresh questions over the "firewall" strategy, under which the other main parties refuse to enter coalition agreements with it.

Merz has struggled

Elected last year on a promise of reforms to return Germany's stagnant economy to growth, Merz has struggled to win over voters, compounding resentment over unpopular pension, tax and healthcare reforms with a stream of communication missteps.

Disillusion with his government has hung over the campaigns in both Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin, where voters have focused on issues including soaring energy and housing costs. Merz presented a consumer relief package on Friday that included tax cuts on gas and diesel.

Several people who voted in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania said living costs were a major concern.

"Here in Schwerin, with these wages, you can hardly afford anything anymore," voter Carlotta Heick told Reuters in the state capital.

One elderly man criticised funding for foreign aid.

"We need our money here, for our country, for children and pensioners," he said, asking not to give his name.

title: Motor neurone disease rates are rising. This new clinic hopes to stop it at the start
text:
In Brief The Brain Institute and Clinic will bring together researchers and clinicians who specialise in motor neurone disease.

MND impacts the brain and neurons that control muscles, leading to progressive weakness and eventual paralysis.

As the rates of a once-rare neurological disease rise, it is hoped that Australia's first combined institute and clinic focused on brain diseases will help find an effective treatment.

On Monday, Macquarie University will launch its Brain Institute and Clinic to bring together researchers and clinicians who specialise in motor neurone disease (MND) to understand its origins and how to treat it.

MND impacts parts of a person's brain and neurons that control their muscles, leading to progressive weakness and eventual paralysis.

It can affect adults of any age and most cases are not genetic.

Macquarie University deputy vice-chancellor Patrick McNeil noted there was still no effective cure for the deadly disease, despite it becoming increasingly common.

The purpose of the institute was to find treatments and deliver them to patients more quickly, he said.

"It typically takes an average of 17 years between when an important research discovery is made ... and when that is implemented in the clinic," McNeill told the Australian Associated Press.

"When you have integrated research and clinical institutions, that journey is shortened."

READ MORE I was researching motor neurone disease, then I was diagnosed with it myself

Earlier this month, NSW became the first jurisdiction in the world to make MND notifiable, meaning medical professionals are now legally required to report cases to the government.

McNeil said he hoped the decision would help researchers better understand the cause.

"It would be good if the other states follow because that is the way that you can find if there is an environmental agent," he said.

"Because what we have been seeing anecdotally is these clusters of cases that seem to be more frequent in a particular town or region than you would expect."

Dominic Rowe, who heads up Macquarie's Neurology Clinic, said 800 Australians would die from the disease this year.

"But I actually disagree with using the term die; motor neuron disease kills you," he said.

"We need to redouble our efforts into working out why so we can fix it."

The facility will also do research and treatment around Parkinson's disease and dementia, including Alzheimer's disease.

Macquarie University professor James Burrell said he was hopeful experts could build on recent breakthroughs in dementia treatment.

He said there were therapies available that slowed the physical progression of dementia caused by Alzheimer's.

"We now have disease-modifying therapies for this disease, and this gives me tremendous hope that we can identify disease-modifying therapies for other neurodegenerative diseases as well," Burrell said.

title: China's 13-year-old swimming prodigy Yu Zidi makes waves at Asian Games
text:
In brief 13-year-old swimmer Yu Zidi was fastest in the women's 200m butterfly heats.

The first gold medal of the 20th Asian Games was won on Sunday by host nation Japan's triathlete, Takumi Hojo.

A 13-year-old swimmer from China has kicked off the 20th Asian Games in blistering form.

Yu Zidi, who does not turn 14 until next month, was fastest by far in the women's 200m butterfly heats.

The Games, being held in Japan, were officially declared open on Saturday by Japan's Emperor Naruhito although there were a large number of empty seats at the 30,000-capacity stadium in Nagoya.

It sounded the starting pistol on two weeks of intense action as the continent's finest athletes compete in more than 40 sports before the curtain comes down on October 4. As always at the Asian Games — which started in 1951 — Olympic staples such as athletics and swimming will sit side-by-side with regional favourites like sepak takraw and kabaddi.

In the swimming pool, Chinese teenager Yu touched almost 2.70 seconds ahead of compatriot Chang Mohan in the butterfly heats and will be a hot favourite to take her first major gold in Sunday evening's final.

China's men's 100m freestyle world record holder and Olympic champion Pan Zhanle also went through fastest to the final in 48.07sec, but was only 0.06sec quicker than South Korea's Hwang Sun-woo.

Meanwhile the first gold medal of the 20th Asian Games was won on Sunday by host nation Japan when Takumi Hojo won the men's individual triathlon in Gamagori city near Nagoya with China's Zhang Xirui second and Kazakhstan's Arlan Zhanabay taking bronze.

It was the first of 469 gold medals to be awarded at a two-week spectacle that has more athletes than the Olympics.

READ MORE IOC lifts ban on Russian athletes, paving the way for 2028 Games return

Hojo finished the 750m swim, 20km bike ride and 5,000m run in 52min 56sec, nine seconds clear of Zhang with Zhanabay a further six seconds behind in third.

"As it's our first gold medal, it's given the Japanese team a real boost," said the 30-year-old Hojo, whose win will qualify him for the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.

"I was really fired-up. Even the rain held off, and I was in top form right up until I stood on the starting line."

China turned the tables later in the women's individual triathlon, where Lin Xinyu improved on her silver medal at the last Asian Games in Hangzhou by winning in 57min 37sec.

Huang Anqi completed a China one-two, 21 seconds behind, with Japan's Manami Hayashi taking the bronze in 58:36.

Dogged by problems

The event in Nagoya and Aichi prefecture has 2028 Olympics places up for grabs but it has been dogged by a series of problems in the build-up.

Accommodating the more than 11,000 athletes and 6,000 officials has stretched organisers to the limit after they decided not to have a traditional athletes' village to save money.

Competitors instead are staying in a combination of temporary container-style huts, hotels and cruise ship the Costa Serena.

Some athletes were left stranded at the airport when transport failed to turn up and several teams have complained about the quality of the huts, including the beds being too short.

title: After a lifetime of achievement, Naomi Watts is just getting started
text:
Advertisement

CultureMoviesFilm Festivals After a lifetime of achievement, Naomi Watts is just getting started Stephanie Bunbury Updated September 23, 2026 — 2:17pm ,first published 12:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Naomi Watts was clearly thrilled to be getting a lifetime achievement award at the San Sebastian Film Festival this week but, after managing to put a stop to the audience’s thunderous applause, she admitted it felt a bit odd. “It’s very strange when you’re in the middle of the journey,” said the one-time star of Australian soap Home and Away. “If anything, I feel I’m just getting started.” Watts, who moved to Hollywood in her early 20s on the strength of her success in Australian films such as Flirting (1991), recalled in her acceptance speech scrabbling for work for 10 years before the late David Lynch cast her as the lead in the seminal film Mulholland Drive. “It wasn’t a smooth ride,” she said. “A lot of people were telling me I wasn’t going to make it. I was too this or not enough of that, not right for this or that: I was always being told what I couldn’t do. But I just kept going; I had this resilience. It was a full 10 years of rejection.” Naomi Watts receives the Donostia lifetime achievement award at the San Sebastian Film Festival. AP Lynch believed in her, she says, before she fully believed in herself. “He saw me and all those wounds from those rejections now appeared as growth. He changed my life.” Every day making that film was fun, she says. “He gave me a different understanding of what it meant to act, to embrace instinct and uncertainty, to not be afraid of the strange or unexplained.” She dedicated her Donostia – the award takes the Basque name for San Sebastian – to him. The success of Mulholland Drive meant that she was seen and then sought out by other top directors including Peter Jackson, Clint Eastwood, Alejandro Gomez Inarritu and David Cronenberg. Spanish director JA Bayona, who directed her Oscar-nominated performance in The Impossible as a mother trapped with her children in the 2004 Thai tsunami. Introducing her to the awards audience, he remembered how she put her trust in him, even though he was new to the game.

Advertisement

Sudden success brought a new episode of discouragement. She was, apparently, almost too old to capitalise on her success. “I was 31 in Mulholland Drive and was told that I’d better get my skates on, because it all finishes at 40. Now here I am, in my late 50s.” Only last week, she pointed out, there were several women over 50 in the Emmy nomination lists. “I do think things have changed. Women are consumers of film and TV and deserve to see their stories reflected,” she said in a press conference for her latest film, The Housewife. “I’m grateful to be part of that shift.” While there are major directors still on her bucket list – in her press conference, she mentioned Paul Thomas Anderson – Watts declared herself still just as excited about working with first-time directors such as Ben Shirinian, who directed her in The Housewife, which is showing in competition in San Sebastian. Set in 1964 and based closely on a real case, the film relates how a cookie-baking, church-going Austrian immigrant was exposed by The New York Times, after a tip-off by Simon Wiesenthal, as a former guard at two concentration camps. Naomi Watts poses during a photocall for her new film The Housewife as it premieres at Spain’s San Sebastian Film Festival. AP “The duality of that woman, living with that secret, was interesting to me as an actor,” she said. At the same time, it was possibly the most difficult role she had ever done, starting with the “shock and awe” she felt reading the script and then researching her abominable crimes. “It was hard to be in that mindset on a daily basis,” she told the press conference. “Anyone here could tell you how conflicted I was after each scene, especially in darker moments.” At a time when hate is on the rise “and it’s a very scary time globally”, she said, cinema and the stories it can tell are more important than ever. Her character Hermine Ryan arrived in the United States at a time when the country supported her belief that it was a place where anyone could start afresh and become what they wanted. Watts herself went to the US, she said, “with hopes and dreams – and way surpassed them”. She has now lived there for decades, discernible in the rolling American “r” sounds that slip in between her Australian vowels and crisp English consonants.

Advertisement

Related Article Vale Elephant Man to Twin Peaks: The six essential David Lynch works Pressed on the state of her adopted nation, she pointed out that she had two American children with actor and former partner Liev Schreiber. “I do love America,” she said in her press conference. “What’s going on today is complicated and nerve-racking, but I have faith things will work out in time.” One of her children identifies as transgender. “I’m proud to be a part of the LGBTQ community,” she said. “Minorities are being attacked right now, and it’s frightful and unacceptable. My heart is with these communities, particularly my family. I’ll do whatever I can to stick up for minorities.” Standing in front of thousands of people – almost all locals – in San Sebastian, however, she recalled her last visit 17 years ago, when The Impossible screened to the home crowd. “The people of San Sebastian are obviously avid film-goers,” she said, “so I’m happy to be here to celebrate with this compelling audience. And I think of the young girl who dreamed of becoming an actor. How is it even possible that I dreamed standing here, three and nearly four decades later? It’s mindblowing.” Must-see movies, interviews and all the latest from the world of film delivered to your inbox. Sign up for our Screening Room newsletter.

title: Why Dockers fans are putting tape on their team’s guernseys
text:
Advertisement

Fremantle MP Josh Wilson has joined Tame Impala frontman Kevin Parker as the latest Dockers fan to jump on a protest against oil and gas giant Woodside’s sponsorship of the club ahead of this weekend’s grand final match. The federal Labor MP, who was taken to the wire by an independent campaign at the last election, was pictured wearing a Dockers guernsey with the Woodside logo covered up in a widely circulated social media post. Federal Labor MP Josh Wilson, centre, pictured with a taped-over Woodside logo on his Dockers guernsey. Tame Impala frontman Kevin Parker (right) also taped over the logo at a concert in Denver last week. And the company’s headquarters in Perth has also been targeted by activists. In a statement, Wilson said the picture in question was a family photo, and “when I wear my Dockers gear I just want to show my support for Freo”. “This week is all about the opportunity to see the Dockers compete on the last Saturday in September, but it’s great that Australia is a place where people have the freedom to express their view and values through a range of creative and peaceful campaigns,” he said.

Advertisement

The move could put Wilson at odds with his Labor colleagues, both federal and state, who have approved a major extension to Woodside’s North West Shelf gas project, and have been open about their support for gas to play a big role as the nation moves away from coal-fired power. It echoes a similar protest by Parker, the Dockers’ No.1 ticketholder, whose love for his hometown team has been on full display as the band tours the United States. Parker was pictured during a concert at Ball Arena in Denver wearing a Dockers top – again, with the Woodside logo covered over by tape. The protests form part of a growing campaign that has reignited calls for the club to drop Woodside’s sponsorship, following in the footsteps of a similar push in 2023, before the Dockers inked another two-year sponsorship deal the following year. The Get Off My Chest campaign has also sprayed over the Woodside logo on a mural of players Michael Walters and Nat Fyfe that adorns the wall of the Fremantle Markets tourist hotspot.

Advertisement

And, with the help of a projector last week, the activists broadcast another message below the giant “Wharfie Time” banner hanging from Woodside’s Perth headquarters, adding “for a gas tax” to the side of the building. Related Article Fremantle Dockers Tame Impala frontman reignites calls for end to Woodside’s Dockers sponsorship For its part, Woodside has shown no intent to back down from its long-running sponsorship of the team, despite the pressure. “We love our partnership of more than 15 years with the Fremantle Football Club and it’s great to see the success the club is having this year,” a spokesperson said when asked about Wilson’s photo. “We’re looking forward to continuing our work together.”

Advertisement

Still, if fans flocking to the port city on Saturday are desperate for a reprieve from the oil and gas giant’s advertising, they may find solace in the (mostly) environmentally conscious local council’s policies. The City of Fremantle adopted a policy last year that “does not support advertising of or by companies involved in the production or supply of fossil fuels owned or managed by the City”. “The City of Fremantle does not support advertising which specifically promotes fossil fuels on property owned or managed by the City,” the policy states. There is a caveat that fossil fuel ads may be displayed during or to promote an event as part of a sponsorship agreement, but it must not be displayed more than 48 before the event, and must be removed within 48 hours of the event’s conclusion. It’s worth noting that Fremantle Oval, in the heart of the CBD, where thousands of Dockers fans will converge on Saturday, is owned by the local council.

“The City of Fremantle is firmly focused on delivering a great Grand Final day experience for Dockers fans this Saturday,” a City of Fremantle spokesperson said. “The City of Fremantle does not support advertising of or by companies involved in production or supply of fossil fuels on property owned or managed by the City and will not accept sponsorship funding from companies involved in production or supply of fossil fuels.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. title: Nat Thaipun is laying the foundations to help you become a better, more instinctive cook

Through her new recipe column, The Foundations, Nat hopes to instil the confidence to cook any type of food – and to stop you being so hard on yourself.

Ever tried your hand at making a curry from scratch, only for it go disastrously wrong? Maybe it’s too salty, or too sweet, perhaps the sauce splits, or turns out weak, watery or unbalanced. For cooking novices, it can often feel easier to just order a takeaway than labour over a new skill.

But Good Food’s new recipe columnist Nat Thaipun insists that imperfection is an integral step in mastering the art of home cooking.

Good Food’s columnist Nat Thaipun with her first Foundations recipe: Panang curry butter sauce. Dion Georgopoulos

“I want to give people the confidence to cook not just Thai food but any kind of food, and not be hard on themselves” says the former MasterChef Australia winner and cookbook author. “Often I find people not wanting to cook because they feel like they’re doing the wrong thing.”

Adapting and allowing room for error are all part of the process, as explored in Thaipun’s new Good Food column, The Foundations. Whether you’re a rookie in the kitchen or know your way around a pan, she will demonstrate a new technique to help build your confidence and form the building blocks necessary to get creative with cooking. Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Critical Resources surges on first-mover Suriname gold grab Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward September 23, 2026 — 1:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Critical Resources has planted its flag in South America after striking a savvy deal for the exclusive right to acquire a 90 per cent interest in the Gonini gold project in Suriname. The move gives the company a rare first-mover advantage for an ASX-listed junior, establishing a foothold in the highly prospective Guiana Shield gold province. And the market appeared to greet the news with a loud cheer, pushing the company’s share price as much as 29 per cent higher to 0.9 of a cent in early trade, on the biggest turnover in more than three months. Excavator-assisted artisanal workings at the Gonini gold project in Suriname, South America pictured in 2020. A geological province Critical Resources says is analogous to West Africa’s prolific Birimian gold belts. The 164-square-kilometre project comprises two granted exploitation rights in the historic Sara Creek gold district, a region with a 150-year history of artisanal and small-scale mining but, notably, no record of modern, systematic exploration. Under the terms of the heavily bank-ended deal, Critical will pay a US$50,000 (A$70,300) signing fee, followed by a completion payment of US$200,000 (A$281,250) in cash and 10 million Critical Resources shares. A series of deferred cash payments totalling US$1.75 (A$2.46) million are payable over the subsequent four years to the vendor, N.V. Gonini Mining Company.

Advertisement

‘This is a gold province with major mines, major discoveries and growing strategic investment.’ Critical Resources managing director Tim Wither Critical has also committed to a minimum exploration expenditure of US$2.5 (A$3.52) million over five years. The vendor will retain a 10 per cent free-carried interest to a decision to mine, in addition to a 2 per cent net smelter return royalty that the company can buy back. The Gonini project sits within the Marowijne greenstone belt, which is proven elephant country. The project lies just 66 kilometres from Newmont’s massive 5.1-million-ounce Merian mine and 88km from Zijin Mining’s 5.6-million-ounce Rosebel operation. The company is quick to point out that mineralisation at those mines is not necessarily indicative of what it might find at Gonini, but the address is undeniably first-class. Critical says the project area straddles the contact between the Paramaka greenstone belt and a tonalite-granodiorite intrusive, a geological setting associated with orogenic gold mineralisation elsewhere in the region. Notably, since the Gonini project comes with granted exploitation rights, the company will have immediate access for exploration, mining, processing and the sale of minerals, avoiding the lengthy processes often required to convert an exploration permit into a mining right.

Advertisement

Critical Resources managing director Tim Wither said: “We believe Gonini gives Critical Resources a rare first-mover position on the ASX: a large, granted gold tenure package in Suriname at a time when global mining capital is increasingly recognising the discovery potential of the Guiana Shield. This is a gold province with major mines, major discoveries and growing strategic investment - but still a fraction of the modern exploration maturity seen elsewhere along the Guiana Shield greenstone belt.” Critical’s entry into Suriname comes at a time when the region is heating up, with major international mining companies and strategic investors increasingly recognising its gold discovery potential. The Guiana Shield, which also covers neighbouring Guyana and French Guiana, is the geological counterpart to West Africa’s famously rich Birimian Greenstone Belt, which has so far coughed up a staggering 500 million ounces of gold. While Critical may be one of the first on the ASX to offer exposure to the region, it is, nevertheless, following a trail blazed by its North American-listed peers. Canadian-listed explorers such as Founders Metals, Miata Metals and Greenheart Gold have all attracted significant strategic capital from mining giants including Gold Fields and La Mancha after unearthing high-grade gold on Surinamese ground. Elsewhere, the company continues to roll out its Mavis Lake lithium project in Canada, home to an 8Mt resource at 1.07 per cent lithium oxide. It also holds an option over solid-state battery-technology intellectual property and has licensed thermal management tech targeting AI high-density electronics data centres. Additionally, Critical holds the Halls Peak base metals project in New South Wales featuring an inferred resource of 840,000 tonnes at 3.7 per cent zinc, 1.5 per cent lead and 0.44 per cent copper. At the same time, it is advancing a growing portfolio of gold, antimony and tungsten prospects across a 1694-square-kilometre ground package in New Zealand.

Advertisement

Gonini features a history of artisanal workings that have exposed weathered bedrock, giving Critical a ready-made starting point for exploration. The company plans to get boots on the ground after the deal is finalised, which is slated within the next 90 days. Its first field campaign is expected to channel-sample exposed pit walls, saprolite and weathered bedrock before rolling into geochemistry, trenching and targeted geophysics. Initial soil lines are planned across the interpreted greenstone-batholith contact, with auger sampling to help peer beneath the deep tropical weathering profile. With a swag of ASX-listed companies now trying to get a foothold in West Africa’s Birimian Shield, it is perhaps more than curious that its geological cousin in South America has been largely overlooked. Now, with a solid ground position, advanced tenure and a clear playbook in a region that is starting to deliver for others, Critical Resources has given itself every chance to change that story. The tribunal upheld the Western Australian Planning Commission’s 2020 rejection of the North Stoneville structure plan, agreeing the risks posed to lives by such a massive influx in population in such a bushfire prone area was unacceptable. The Tribunal said the structure plan did not adhere with state bushfire planning policy, which prioritised the preservation of life and the strict management of bushfire impacts in planning.

“Section 2 of SPP 3.7 provides that the preservation of life and the management of bushfire impact are ‘paramount’ and, as we have been at pains to reiterate, SPP 3.7 and the guidelines require the management of bushfire risk, where it cannot be avoided altogether, to an acceptable level,” it said in its decision. “We find that the structure plan does not demonstrate that that can be done on the site. “Indeed, in our view the structure plan proceeds on the basis of such basic flaws that it cannot be ‘saved’ by the making of modifications. “Our finding is that the structure plan put before us and relied upon by Satterley is so flawed as to warrant a refusal to approve it.” A spokeswoman for Satterley Group said the company was disappointed with the decision but would need to review the judgment.

WAPC lawyers also revealed Satterley had offered to only build 135 lots at the site until road improvements were complete. The tribunal, however, flagged that its decision did not mean the area was not suitable for urban development.

Urbanisation of North Stoneville has been ferociously rejected by the surrounding community since it was first floated in 1991. It has also been rejected by the Shire of Mundaring council, the Department of Fire and Emergency Services, in more than 4000 public submissions, and twice by WA’s highest planning authority since 2020. The community opposition revolves around the loss of native bushland and fire risk. The WAPC rejected the most recent North Stoneville structure plan in December 2023 because of the bushfire risk.
